#6390. A Brief-ish History of METI. Part IV: Millennial METI Experiments

Welcome back to our ongoing series on the Brief-ish History of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI). In our previous installments, we examined the inspiration and earliest experiments in this field. We then looked at how it co-evolved with the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI), leading to the first true attempt to send a message of greeting to the stars (the Arecibo Message). We followed up with a look at two of the brightest minds in the business (Frank Drake and Carl Sagan), the brains behind the first interstellar messages (the Pioneer Plaques and the Voyager Golden Records).

Today, we'll look at experiments conducted since the end of the Space Age and the turn of the century. And just like SETI, the number of experiments has grown considerably, thanks to renewed interest in space exploration following new efforts to explore Mars and the Solar System. This included the first orbital observatory, the venerable Hubble Space Telescope, and deep space probes like the Galileo, Cassini-Huygens, Magellan, and Venus Express missions.

This era also saw revitalized efforts to search for signs of past (and maybe present) life on Mars. These included orbiters like the Mars Odyssey and Mars Express missions, and rovers and landers like Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, as well as Spirit and Opportunity. These experiments also reflected the changing nature of space exploration, which included missions from emerging space agencies, non-profits, and private entities.

All of these experiments built on the legacy of the Arecibo Message, adding additional information and personal touches where the creators desired.

An explanatory diagram of a message transmitted in 1983 by Masaki Morimoto and Hisashi Hirabayashi to Altair. Credit: ShizuShizu/Wikimedia

In 1983, astronomers Masaaki Morimoto and Hisashi Hirabayashi used the Stanford Dish radio telescope at Stanford University to transmit the Message to Altair (or the Call to the Cosmos 83'). The message was produced in collaboration with the Japanese publication Weekly Shonen Jump and transmitted on August 15th, 1983, to commemorate the publication's 15th anniversary. The destination was Altair, an A-type blue-white giant star located 16.7 light-years from Earth, which represents the Shinto deity Hikoboshi in the Tanabata legend.

Like the Arecibo Message, the content was a symbolic, graphic message meant to convey information about humanity, life on Earth, and peace. Unlike the Arecibo message, the Message to Altair consisted of several pages rather than a single, long pictograph, each dealing with a different subject. The first page included mathematical information, such as the numbers 1 to 12, prime numbers, powers of 3, formulas for indicating addition and multiplication, and chemical elements essential to life.

For this, Morimoto and Hirabayashi chose hydrogen, helium, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen, the building blocks of stars and planetary systems. Several other molecules were included, including hydroxide, water, nitrous oxide, formaldehyde, hydrogen cyanide, and their respective wavelengths. All of these chemicals play a central role in prebiotic chemistry and the formation of organic molecules that give rise to life.

Page two included information on the Solar System, including (from top to bottom) the Sun, the planets in order of distance, some of the larger moons, and their equatorial radii and mean distances from the Sun. Pages three and four included the chemical formulae for DNA compounds, as well as showing DNA structure and replication. This was followed by a series of drawings that showed different types of life forms on Earth, and they were arranged to convey the process of biological evolution.

They begin with pictures of early primitive life, followed by jellyfish, fish, amphibians, lizards, early mammals, apes, and then humans. Like the Pioneer Plaques, this image shows a man and a woman with two children between them. This was followed by a close-up illustration of the woman's face waving hello. The last page showed the transmission parameters: the total number of bits, the transmission wavelength, and the radius of the radio telescope that beamed the message.

It also contained the Japanese and English spelling for the word "toast," followed by the chemical formula for ethanol alcohol - in short, the message concludes with the raising of a toast with an alcoholic drink.

The thirteen pictures that make up the Message to Altair, listed in order (left to right, top to bottom). Credit: Shinya Nurasawa

As Altair is approximately 17 light-years distant, the message would have arrived around 2000, and the window for a reply would open by 2017. In 2023, Hyogo University astronomer Shin-ya Narusawa (who knew Morimoto before his death) asked the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) to help search for a possible reply. JAXA obliged and used the radio antenna at the Usuda Space Observatory to observe Altair for an hour at 10 p.m. on August 22nd, 2023.

The date was significant because it also fell on Tanabata in the old Japanese calendar and is the only day of the year when the deities Orihime and Hikoboshi (represented by Vega and Altair, respectively) are allowed to meet. The observations detected no signals, but Narusawa said he intends to continue observing and collaborating with other research institutions.

Between 1999 and 2003, three METI experiments were conducted using the Evpatoria Planetary Radar (EPR), a Soviet-era facility located in the Crimea for deep-space communications and radio astronomy. All four projects were organized with help from famed Soviet-Russian radio engineer, astronomer, and SETI researcher Alexander Zaitsev. As we addressed in part I of the series, he coined the term METI in his 2006 paper, Messaging to Extra-Terrestrial Intelligence.

The first project to use the EPR RT-70 radio telescope was the Cosmic Call, which included two broadcasts, one sent in 1999 and the other in 2003. The venture was a crowdsourced effort by Texas-based startup Team Encounter, Canadian astrophysicist Yvan Dutil, Russian scientists (including Zaitsev), and Eastern European radio engineers.

The message included contributions by Dutil and his fellow physicist StÃ©phane Dumas. Their primer was inspired by Hans Freudenthal's 1960 book Lincos: Design of a Language for Cosmic Intercourse, which describes a language designed to be understandable to an extraterrestrial intelligence (ETI). Using Lincos, Dutil and Dumas' message (DDM) was carefully structured to include pictograms showing mathematics, physics (the hydrogen spectrum), and related concepts.

The second part consisted of a series of pictograms created by Richard Braastad of Team Encounter, the Braastad Message (DM). It used mathematical symbols to describe a solar sail (another project Team Encounter was working on), including its dimensions, payload, trajectory, and projected launch time. This was followed by the original Arecibo Message (AM), the company's Team Encounter 2001 Staff Message (ESM), and a message composed with input from the public - the Public Part (PP).

The second page of the primer prepared by Dutil and Dumas, denoting mathematical concepts (part of the Cosmic Call). Credit: Dumas, S.

The broadcast was broken into four sessions, lasting a total of 40 hours, with each session targeting a different Sun-like (G-type) star system. These included 16 Cygni A on May 24th, 1999, a G-type star in a triple-star system located 69 light-years from Earth. On June 30th, 1999, the target was 15 Sagittae, another G-type star about 58 light-years from Earth in the Sagittarius Constellation. Lastly, and again on June 30th, 1999, the team transmitted to HD 178428, a G-type star located 69 light-years away, also in the Sagittarius Constellation.

Each session of Cosmic Call 1 transmitted the scientific parts (DDM, BM, AM, and ESM) three times at 100 bits per second, followed by the Public Part (PP), sent once at 2000 bits/s. The full message was structured as:

DDM â BM â AM â ESM â DDM â BM â AM â ESM â DDM â BM â AM â ESM â PP

The second Cosmic Call, in 2003, followed a similar structure. For this message, Dutil and Dumas presented an updated version of their Lincos pictographs (DDM2), the Arecibo Message, the Bilingual Image Glossary, and the same Public Part. The structure was as follows:

DDM2 â DDM2 â DDM2 â AM â AM â AM â BIG â BIG â BIG â BM â ESM â PP,

The destinations for this message included five more stars, with all transmissions occurring on the same day (July 6th, 2033). They included GJ 49, a G-type star located 32 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia, on July 6th, 2003. This was followed by Gliese 208, an M-type (red dwarf) star 37 light-years away in the constellation Orion; 55 Cancri, an M-type star 41 light-years away in Cancer; HD 10307, a binary star system with a G-type primary and an M-type companion 42.6 light-years away in Andromeda; and 47 Ursae Majoris, a G-type star located 45.3 light-years away in Ursa Major.

The Cosmic Calls were the most ambitious public SETI/METI effort mounted to date. While Team Encounter went bankrupt in the years that followed, their messages established a precedent that would be joined by several more METI efforts in the new millennium. Zaitsev would play a key role in several, and his work with his colleagues would culminate by 2008 in the creation of METI International. More on that soon!

#6388. Independents decide the election, again!

A group of new senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer’s office in Washington on Monday. The large class of incoming Democratic senators was propelled by votes from independents, Winston writes. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

According to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

Independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also shows that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they showed up.

Looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

For example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

Despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

Overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

Clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

In the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

According to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top issue concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent said it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

The president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent said his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

Trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic issues and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

Neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls showed that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

Independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

At a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent said the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

Democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

David Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy issues, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

#6387. Maybe Dark Energy Isn't so Inexplicable After All

The Universe as we know it is comprised of three "things": baryonic matter (planets, stars, galaxies, us), dark matter (still unexplained) and dark energy (really, really still unexplained). Of the three, dark energy remains the most challenging. It's "something" that's driving the acceleration of the expanding Universe but that's all we know about it. We can't see it, or even put a description to it, other than "it's mysterious".

This cosmic component accounts for about 70 percent of the known Universe's energy budget. Physicists have spent a lot of time trying to explain it, often invoking some hitherto-unknown fields, or exotic physical particles, or some kind of "cosmological constant" that is the same everywhere in space and time. Despite these and other attempts at explaining dark energy, physicists still don't know exactly what it is. However, there's hope that an explanation will come in our lifetimes. A team of scientists at Canada's University of British Columbia and the University of Sheffield (in England) have come up with a possible model that provides an explanation. They think dark matter may be a product of the same physics that governs the strength of the atomic nucleus. If that's true, then they could use the standard model of particle physics to understand this mysterious thing that is pushing the Universe apart.

Dark energy has many descriptions, which reflects our incomplete understanding of it. It could be a negative pressure that pushes space outward, although thereâs no proof of that. It could be vacuum energy, which is an idea that thereâs a background of energy that permeates all of the Universe. Itâs also been called âquintessenceâ, which is a sort of imaginary âfluidâ that fills space. Or it could be a combo of dark matter and dark energy, both yet unexplained. The wildest idea is that dark energy could be a wrinkle in the fabric of space-time, or even something leaking from another universe. All those explanations are fairly wild, and oftentimes in science, the simplest is the best explanation. Thatâs where the work in Canada and England is coming in handy, if particle physics can provide insight.

According to lead scientist Ariel Zhitnitsky of UBC, using particle physics means we don't need exotic explanations for dark energy. âOur theoretical framework suggests no new particles may be required at all,â said Zhitnitsky, who developed the theoretical ideas explained by the team. âThe characteristic energy scale predicted from the QCD vacuum and gravity comes out close to the observed dark-energy scale today without having to introduce an ad hoc new field nor new parameter.â

What Zhitnitsky and others are talking about is a theory called quantum chromodynamics (QCD). It focuses on the strong nuclear force that holds quarks inside the protons and neutrons that make up atoms. QCD describes the actions of the strong force. Those actions could be affecting space, and in particular what it contains.

A NASA illustration of the strong force at work in an atomic nucleus. Credit: NASA

Space is never empty. Rather, itâs filled with subatomic fields and something called quantum energy. That's energy that exists in individual packets called âquantaâ. This creates a âquantum vacuumâ with properties that can affect space over large distances. Now, add in the fact that the Universe is expanding, and that has implications that need further explanation. The team, led by scientist Dong Ha Lee, proposed the following: as the Universe expands, the subatomic structure in the quantum vacuum responds differently as time goes by. That response generates a small energy shift that is just enough to drive the acceleration of universal expansion. The team points out that you donât need new particles or other exotic things for this: the current particles are just fine, Lee suggested. âThe idea that the quantum vacuum as described by QCD could have the right properties to account for the accelerated expansion of the universe is very intriguing,â said Lee.

So, if this idea holds up, it means that dark energy could have a connection to the strong nuclear force. Scientists could create models to test this using currently available physics models. The big test would be to compare it to cosmological data, according to Lee. âOur analysis shows that such a model can reproduce the evolving dark energy behaviour suggested by current observations. This motivates further theoretical work to better understand how the QCD vacuum responds to cosmic expansion and to develop predictions that can be tested with future observations.â

When tested against real astronomical data including light from distant supernovae and leftover radiation from the early Universe, the team found that their model matched observations just as well as standard cosmological models. In addition, it offers a possible way to explain what is causing dark energy. The next step for the team is to keep refining their model and calculations in order to build as robust a model as possible. By that time, observations and data from the next generations of telescopes, such as the Nancy Grace Roman telescope, could prove very useful in testing ideas about the true nature of dark energy and its effects on the expanding Universe over time.

Could Standard Physics Explain the Mysterious Energy Driving the Universe Apart?

#6383. White House warns Democrats against aggressive oversight

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.

The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to issue subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

The letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter says.

Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse," Garcia said. "The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.

"It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.

Last week, President Donald Trump himself said that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

He also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

And Trump last year publicly called for longtime critic Sen. Adam B. Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

Garcia and other Democrats have signaled they intend to pursue oversight aggressively in the new Congress. After Democrats won the House majority last week, Garcia put out an all-caps statement urging administration officials to “LAWYER UP” ahead of the new year.

Garcia, as well as other likely incoming chairs such as House Judiciary ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; Homeland Security ranking member Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., have hinted at broad inquiries ranging from the handling of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to immigration enforcement and more.

Raskin told reporters last week that he thought Democratic oversight efforts could dovetail with the party’s broader effort to address affordability issues, including by addressing the Iran war, allegations of corruption within the Trump administration and more.

“We're going to get all the information that we need in order to restore the rule of law in American constitutional democracy,” Raskin said.

The letter also echoes a previous fight the administration pitched with the House in the first Trump administration, where officials resisted in court allowing former White House Counsel Don McGahn to testify to the House Judiciary Committee for years.

#6377. Why do some images stick in your memory while others fade?

Recordings inside the amygdala show which pictures a person will remember, flagged within a third of a second of first seeing them.

You can look at two pictures for the same length of time and, minutes later, recognize only one. In a new experiment, that difference showed up in the brain about a third of a second after each picture appeared.

Some cells deep in the brain fired more strongly for pictures people later recognized. Those cells sit in the amygdala, a structure better known for fear.

Jiayang Xiao and Ueli Rutishauser of Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles led the work.

They collaborated with colleagues at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, Toronto Western Hospital, and the University of Toronto.

Everyone in the study had drug-resistant epilepsy and was already wired with electrodes, so surgeons could find where the seizures start. The memory test was a run of photographs on a screen, not anything from daily life.

“Our results demonstrate that the activity of specific kinds of neurons in the amygdala predicts, while the person sees an image for the first time, whether that image will later be remembered,” said Rutishauser, who directs the Center for Neural Science and Medicine at Cedars-Sinai.

“Such episodic autobiographical memories, such as where we parked our car or how we spent a recent family vacation, are critical to navigating everyday life and a sense of who we are.”

The amygdala’s reputation comes from fear and feeling. People with damage on both sides of it remember emotional material poorly.

Brain scans going back to the 1990s found that the harder the amygdala worked while someone studied an emotional picture, the better that person held onto it.

So the working explanation was feeling. A strong reaction marks a moment as worth keeping, and the amygdala supplies the reaction.

Xiao’s team asked something narrower. Instead of the amygdala’s overall activity, they tracked single neurons that each answer to one kind of thing.

One cell fires for faces and ignores cars. Another fires for landscapes and ignores food. These are called category cells, and 40% of the amygdala neurons here were one.

The two explanations predict different things. If feeling is the mark, a jolt should lift every cell at once. If the content of the moment is the mark, only the cells tuned to that content should move.

The electrodes used for seizure monitoring carry eight hair-thin wires at the tip. That is fine enough to hear one neuron at a time.

Across 49 sessions with 42 patients, the team logged 1,871 well-isolated neurons. Of those, 575 were in the amygdala and 405 in the hippocampus, the region usually given credit for building memories.

The task was plain. Photographs from five categories – people, food, animals, cars and landscapes – came up for two seconds each, and all of them were new to the patient.

Ten to 30 minutes later came a test of 400 images. Half had been in the earlier run and half had never been seen.

Six buttons were available for each one. Three said new and three said old, and the button within each set said how sure the patient was. Patients got 70.3% right, against 50% for guessing.

When patients first saw the pictures, category cells in the amygdala fired more strongly for images the patients later recognized than for those they didn’t.

The effect held only when the picture belonged to the cell’s own category.

A cell tuned to faces fired more strongly for faces the patient later recognized. When the patient saw a car, that same cell’s activity gave no clue about whether the patient would recognize it later.

The difference in firing appeared about 350 milliseconds after the picture came into view and lasted until about 1,850 milliseconds.

The cells started responding to their preferred category at around 300 milliseconds, just before the first signs of which pictures patients would remember.

The effect held after researchers accounted for an online panel’s ratings of how pleasant and exciting the images were.

The ratings alone did not predict which pictures patients later recognized.

The first dataset also showed a weaker hippocampal signal that emerged around 1,300 milliseconds. In sessions that recorded both regions, the amygdala’s signal was stronger.

Rutishauser told Earth.com that the amygdala finding surprised him because the region is best known for responding to emotionally charged experiences. Here, its activity predicted which neutral images patients would later recognize.

The fusiform gyrus is a patch of visual cortex where two-thirds of the neurons were category cells, the highest share anywhere in the study.

It showed no such split between the pictures that were remembered and the ones that were not. Strong tuning by itself does not do this.

For the kind of memory tested here, Rutishauser said, the memory itself is stored in the hippocampus, and the amygdala works more like a controller.

“The system that produces the hot air (the heater) is separate and distinct from the controller (the thermostat),” he noted to Earth.com. “In analogy, here the amygdala would be the thermostat that controls the memory system.”

The two regions were also in step. Slow electrical waves run through the hippocampus at around 10 cycles a second.

Amygdala cells fired more tightly in time with those waves when a picture was going to be remembered than when it was going to be forgotten.

A second set of recordings, from 95 other patients and 5,744 neurons, carried the amygdala result again. The hippocampal effect did not come back in that one.

Among the pictures patients did recognize, the ones they felt sure about had drawn more firing at first sight than the ones they guessed at.

The team then split each patient’s hits into two kinds of remembering. There is the vivid sort, where a person gets the moment itself back, and the vague sort, where a picture only feels familiar.

The amygdala signal tracked the vivid kind, with a session-by-session correlation of 0.50. It showed no reliable link to familiarity.

The effect was also stronger in the right amygdala than in the left. The authors call that part provisional and say it needs replication.

It may follow from their choice of material, since the right side of the brain is tied to remembering pictures and the left to remembering words.

Nothing here was switched on or off. Every number is a prediction read off a recording, so what the amygdala does for a memory, as opposed to what it says about one, is still open.

The hippocampal effect that showed up in one dataset and not the other is unsettled too.

The patients were also people with epilepsy severe enough to need brain surgery, and the electrodes went where their care required.

Amygdala tissue shrinks early in Alzheimer’s disease, and memory trouble is common in temporal lobe epilepsy.

Rutishauser said the findings are still too preliminary to guide treatment for people with memory problems.

However, he also noted that the research raises the possibility that a device designed to aid memory could target the amygdala, particularly on the right side of the brain.

One possibility is that deep brain stimulation could boost the activity of cells already responding to what a person sees.

The idea is untested. Earlier teams that stimulated the whole amygdala electrically improved recognition of neutral pictures, but none aimed at the category cells.

Rutishauser’s team is now studying how the amygdala coordinates with other brain regions and whether stimulating it can improve memory.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Neuroscience.

#6376. Southern right whales are raising calves in places scientists didn’t expect

Southern right whale mothers off Australia moved to a different nursing bay 54% of the time, crowding into sites where other whales were.

Researchers long thought southern right whales returned to the same bay where they were nursed to raise their own calves.

But off southern Australia, when researchers spotted the same mother with different calves in successive sightings, she was in a different nursing area 54% of the time.

As southern right whales recovered from whaling, mothers and calves gathered in three stretches of coast, while other apparently suitable areas drew few whales.

Researchers think the presence of other whales may help explain why those three areas grew so quickly.

Anne Grundlehner of the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania led the work with colleagues from the Australian Antarctic Division.

Her team used nearly five decades of aerial surveys and a photo catalog that tells individual right whales apart by the rough patches of skin on their heads.

The catalog held 501 females seen with a calf in at least two different years between 1978 and 2012. Nearly two thirds, 63.5%, had nursed in more than one of the ten areas where the whales gather.

Among all 767 whales photographed in more than one year, 82.4% were seen in more than one area.

Mothers did come back to the three busiest areas more often. A mother seen in one of those three with a calf was back with her next calf 48% of the time. In the seven smaller areas, the figure was 15%.

“The results surprised us very much,” Grundlehner said in an interview with Earth.com.

Right whales were long believed to memorize the bay or beach where they were nursed as newborns and to return to it again and again, she said.

A single-engine plane has flown the coast of Western Australia each winter since 1976. The route now runs about 1,550 miles (2,500 kilometers), from Perth to Ceduna in South Australia.

Southern right whales spend summer feeding far to the south and migrate to the coast in winter.

Mothers and calves stay in water 16 to 33 feet (5 to 10 meters) deep, close to the beach.

From 1,500 feet (450 to 500 meters) up, the crew spots almost every dark whale over the pale sand, then drops lower for a photograph.

Flights run from mid-August to mid-September, when calf numbers peak, and the annual count climbed from a handful to several hundred.

“When the whales were still a rarity along the coastline, the few whales visiting our coast seemed randomly distributed across suitable habitat. There weren’t any sites that stood out as hotspots,” Grundlehner said.

By the mid-1980s, southern right whales were gathering in three areas that filled up much faster than the rest of the coast.

The hotspots were Bremer and Doubtful Islands Bays, the stretch from Israelite Bay to Point Culver, and the Bunda Cliffs and Head of Bight.

In one of those areas, the number of mothers with calves rose by about 30% a year during the first decade.

Daughters returning to their birth bays can’t account for growth that fast. The team did the arithmetic.

With every female returning to her birth area, a calf every three years and no deaths, an area’s mothers could grow by at most 9.7% a year.

Which areas were busy at the start didn’t predict which became busy later, either. By a statistical measure of clumping, the whales bunched up more each year until about 2000, and the pattern has held since.

“Instead, as the population grew in numbers, the female whales were more likely to select nursing grounds where there were other whales,” said co-author Stuart Corney, an associate professor at the same institute.

The team’s reading is that mothers rely on a memory of past nursing sites plus the sight or sound of other whales, a pattern also proposed for humpback whales.

The three busy areas are more open and exposed than the other bays, which the authors suggest could make other whales easier to see or hear.

When only a few dozen whales reached the coast each year, there may have been no one to follow.

The whales do seem loyal to something, at a larger scale. Most repeat sightings of the same whale fell within about 620 miles (1,000 kilometers) of each other.

Grundlehner told Earth.com the findings imply more flexibility than researchers had assumed.

Grundlehner was asked what the findings mean for protecting nursing areas.

“This is extremely important for effective conservation management: it means that you should not just protect the places with the highest numbers of an animal species you are trying to protect, but all suitable habitat that is available and accessible to them,” she said.

Areas used by few whales today could matter more if the population grows or if climate change alters the coast, she said. The range also needs to stay connected, with nothing blocking movement between nursing sites.

Growth is not guaranteed. Since about 2015, annual numbers in every area have flattened or dipped, and the population is estimated at a tenth of its pre-whaling size.

Grundlehner’s team reported in a 2025 study that recovery had stalled. She told Earth.com that calf numbers from 2023 to 2026 have stayed relatively stable, about 8% below their peak around 2016 and 2017.

The team can’t rule out other explanations for why some bays filled and others didn’t.

Records from before whaling are patchy, so it’s uncertain whether the three busy areas were busy two centuries ago.

The photo catalog also stops in 2012, so the latest decade of movements hasn’t been checked whale by whale.

And a more flexible whale isn’t necessarily a safer one. A population that follows other whales, or returns to a remembered bay, may keep using a place even after conditions there change, the authors wrote.

What draws whales to a particular bay, including local conditions and human disturbance, has to be worked out.

After that, someone has to watch whether the three crowded areas hold if the population starts growing again or shrinks further.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6375. Another bill to release Epstein files headed to House floor

Massie will force another vote on releasing files in the Jeffrey Epstein case. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

As Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.

Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., was the decisive 218th signature on the discharge petition, a procedural tool allowing rank-and-file House members to register their support for a piece of legislation and circumvent leadership to force a vote. Massie and other supporters of the effort say the bill is a bid for transparency.

Earlier this week, Massie said his pitch to his colleagues was simple.

“They could be a hero if they sign it,” he said, as he chased down the final two signatures as the House returned from recess on Monday. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., signed just before Garamendi.

Massie’s time left in office is ticking down after a challenger backed by President Donald Trump ousted him in his GOP primary earlier this year.

The petition marks the second push led by Massie to require the release of the Epstein files. Last fall, Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., led a discharge petition on a bill dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which directed the Justice Department to publicly release documents in its possession related to Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

The bill passed the House by a vote of 427-1 last November, and in the Senate a few days later. Trump signed the measure shortly afterward.

In a statement this summer, Massie said he believes the Justice Department is still withholding more than 3 million files that it is required to release under the November 2025 law and is “maintaining heavy redactions” on others.

The new bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the federal government for withholding such documents. It would also allow victims to privately view unredacted versions of any records that mention them.

Now that the new petition has reached 218 signatures, it must sit for seven legislative days before being called up by anyone who signed it. Last time around, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., scheduled a House vote on the initial Epstein bill before that ripening period was over, saying it was a foregone conclusion that the legislation would reach the floor.

Other Republicans who have signed on to the petition this year include Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C.; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., none of whom will be returning next Congress. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., backed the initial effort last fall, but her name did not appear on the petition this time.

Allies of the issue in Congress have faced pushback from Trump. While the president suggested during his 2024 reelection campaign that he was open to declassifying some Epstein documents, Trump then shifted gears, calling them a “hoax.”

“Once you get to 218, you can never sign it," Massie said. "There's nobody left, no spots left. It goes straight to the floor, and then you can vote for it. But you were never part of the group that actually got it to the floor."

#6374. Honey bee hives can lose their most destructive pest at high altitudes

Low oxygen levels at high altitudes prevent varroa mites from reproducing, offering a potential way to protect honeybees.

Varroa mites kill honey bee colonies around the world. Beekeepers fight them with chemical treatments year after year.

On the Tibetan Plateau, however, hives have gone untreated since 2006. Beekeepers there report that the mites simply disappear.

At two sites above about 11,500 feet (3,500 meters), low oxygen pressure kept the mites’ young from maturing.

A lack of oxygen had never before been shown to stop the mite from breeding. The finding could lead to new ways of controlling the pest without chemicals.

The work was led by Huoqing Zheng of Zhejiang University. Researchers at the Xizang Academy of Agriculture and Animal Husbandry Sciences in Lhasa took part. So did scientists at the University of Salford in England.

Infested hives were trucked to different heights in China. The high-altitude effect was then copied in hives close to sea level.

That second test was small, with five hives over 11 days. The team also hasn’t yet worked out how low oxygen stops the mites.

“For the first time, beekeepers in Tibet noticed the parasitic varroa mite mysteriously disappear from their colonies,” the authors wrote in a statement.

“We found that the low oxygen pressure on the Tibetan Plateau prevents the mites from reproducing.”

Honey bees are the most important managed pollinator of farm crops. For 60 years, Varroa destructor has been a leading cause of their deaths.

A female mite enters a cell holding a bee larva about a day before the cell is sealed. Worker bees close it with a wax cap. Shut inside, the mite feeds on the larva. Her first egg is laid about 60 hours later.

The first egg always becomes a male. The next three or four become females. They mate with their brother inside the cell.

Time in a worker bee’s cell is limited. Only the male and up to three daughters grow up before the bee emerges. Only the adult daughters can survive outside, where they live and feed on adult bees.

Mite populations can grow rapidly once a colony becomes infested. Viruses are also transmitted by the mites as they feed. In cooler regions this combination can kill a colony within three years.

In China, hives are treated with chemicals up to five times a year. Despite these treatments, high colony losses continue to be reported. The mite has been identified as the main cause of these losses.

Beekeeping on the plateau began only recently. In 2004 a total of 30 colonies were brought up to the region. Twenty years later the number of colonies had grown to more than 12,000.

In May 2024 a total of 60 colonies were taken from a single apiary in southern China. The colonies were divided into four groups of 15 for the experiment.

One group was moved to another site in Xishuangbanna at roughly 1,800 feet (554 meters). The remaining three groups were transported by truck to sites located at higher elevations.

Kunming lies at roughly 6,450 feet (1,966 meters) and Nyingchi lies at roughly 9,600 feet (2,928 meters).

The highest site was Lhasa at roughly 11,900 feet (3,637 meters), more than twice the elevation of Denver.

A decline in mite infestation was observed only in the Lhasa group. Before the move, mites were present in 9.3% of developing bees in the colonies headed for Lhasa.

This proportion had decreased to 1.6% after four months and no mites were detected after one year. No treatment had been applied to these hives. Instead the offspring of the mites failed to reach adulthood.

An increase in infestation was recorded at the lower sites over the same period.

In Kunming, the proportion of infested bees increased from 2.8% to 21.8% within two months. Those colonies were also attacked by hornets.

The elevation of Nyingchi proved insufficient to provide protection. Infestation there increased from 3.4% to 10.6% over four months and all colonies had died within a year.

By the four-month mark, 25 of the 30 colonies at the two lowest sites had died. Mites were considered the most likely cause of these losses.

In contrast, 14 of the 15 Lhasa colonies remained alive and free of mites after one year. Thirteen of these colonies survived for two years without any treatment.

To see what was going wrong, the team opened sealed cells with forceps. Each cell was checked under a flashlight, and young mites were counted in at least 218 infested cells per group.

Mother mites in Lhasa never laid more than two eggs. A second high site, tested in 2023, showed the same thing. Those eggs seldom developed into the next stage.

Across 178 cells with older pupae at both sites, no daughter mite was on track to become a mated adult.

It all happened fast. Just three days after the trucks arrived in Lhasa, mothers were laying far fewer eggs. By day six, each was laying one or two eggs that never developed.

The team also looked for other explanations. Bees keep the brood nest at a steady warmth whatever the weather.

Nests in both Lhasa and Xishuangbanna stayed at about 93°F to 94°F (34°C), and humidity was similar too.

Worker bees took about 21 days from egg to adult in both places, so altitude had not slowed them. The lowland colonies had been trucked as well.

Yet in Lhasa, mite breeding stayed low for months after the hives stopped moving.

That left oxygen as a possible explanation. At Lhasa’s high altitude, oxygen pressure is only about two-thirds of that at sea level.

A second experiment was designed to test the role of oxygen directly. Low-oxygen hives were set up in Shaoxing in eastern China at about 290 feet (88 meters) above sea level.

A nitrogen-rich gas mixture was supplied from a cylinder to each of five small hives. The hives were wrapped in cling film to reduce leakage of the gas.

The flow was adjusted by hand whenever the oxygen readings moved outside the target range. The entrances were left open so that the bees could continue to forage.

Each hive was first kept on ordinary air and then switched to air with roughly Lhasa’s oxygen level. Under ordinary air the mother mites produced an average of 3.9 offspring.

After 11 days under low oxygen this figure fell to 1.7. Almost none of these offspring developed beyond the egg stage.

Eleven days after their cells were sealed, the worker bees examined in both conditions had reached the newly emerged adult stage.

This fits with honey bees being known to forage as high as about 13,450 feet (4,100 meters). A similar decline in mite reproduction had been seen after six days in a 2023 trial with six hives.

Adult mites appear to tolerate low oxygen better than their offspring. In Lhasa the mother mites remained in the hives for several months although they could not reproduce.

An adult mite breathes through two networks of air tubes. Each network opens to the outside through a single pore. Adult females have also been reported to move air through these tubes by changing their body volume.

Newly hatched mites have no air tubes at all. Instead they absorb oxygen through the skin until the first molt, when the tubes are formed.

Most young mites in Lhasa failed to develop beyond this first stage. The authors suggest that this feature may contribute to the vulnerability of the young. This explanation has not yet been tested.

A similar pattern has been reported in fruit flies and in a common spider mite. In both species egg production is more sensitive to low oxygen than adult survival.

Other mechanisms may also be involved, such as the mother’s energy reserves or how cells use and sense oxygen. These possibilities are listed by the authors as questions for future work.

Moving hives to such high elevations is not practical for most beekeepers. The team therefore tested a simple and low-cost alternative.

Hive entrances were narrowed at night so that the breathing of the bees lowered the oxygen inside. In a pilot test this method partly reduced mite reproduction. “This physiological limit of varroa mites opens new avenues of controlling this globally destructive pest,” the authors wrote.

All of the results so far come from hives in China. Only one kind of bee was studied, the Italian honey bee, the type most commonly kept there.

The effect has not yet been tested in other regions or with other kinds of bees.

It is also unclear whether lowland hives can stay low in oxygen long enough to stop mites safely. The bees themselves would need to remain unharmed.

Future research could test whether narrowing hive entrances keeps mite numbers down over a full season.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Biology.

#6373. Satellites measure a changing Earth with help from a laser in the Arctic

A laser station in Svalbard tracks satellites as they pass over the Arctic, helping scientists measure changes in ice and sea level.

Today’s Image of the Day looks down on the west coast of Spitsbergen, where glaciers reach the sea and tan streaks cut through turquoise water.

Near the shore of one of those fjords, a research station does much of its work in the opposite direction. It aims a laser into the sky to find out exactly where satellites are as they pass overhead.

Landsat 9 captured this view of Norway’s Svalbard archipelago on July 30, 2026.

The laser system at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory officially debuted that October.

It’s the northernmost satellite laser ranging facility in the world, a distinction that matters because of how often some satellites pass within reach.

Imagine tracing a line around a globe that passes close to both poles. Turn the globe a little and draw another line along the same path.

The two lines cross the equator far apart, but they come close together in the far north. As Earth rotates beneath a satellite in a near-polar orbit, its path over the ground follows much the same pattern.

That gives Ny-Ålesund more chances to track the same satellite. NASA’s station in Greenbelt, Maryland, might catch a polar-orbiting satellite two or three times a day.

At Ny-Ålesund, a satellite on that kind of route can come within view on almost every orbit.

The Arctic station also fills a geographic gap in a network of more than 40 laser ranging stations around the world.

The station sends a short pulse of light toward a satellite equipped with special reflectors.

Some of that light returns to a detector on the ground. Since scientists know how fast light travels, they can convert the round-trip time to a distance.

Half the total distance traveled is the range from the station to the satellite. A series of those measurements helps researchers work out the satellite’s path.

The new system can send thousands of pulses a second, compared with tens per second for older equipment.

Its detector is sensitive enough to register a single photon, the smallest unit of light. That matters because a satellite may send back only a tiny fraction of the light that leaves the ground.

A faster laser gives the station more chances to collect those faint returns during a pass.

One satellite that can benefit from the Svalbard station is ICESat-2. It carries a laser of its own and points it down to measure the height of ice sheets, sea ice and other surfaces.

In that case, the satellite times light returning from Earth. At Ny-Ålesund, the station times light returning from the satellite.

The two measurements answer different questions that matter to the same mission.

To see why, imagine measuring the height of a glacier from an aircraft. Knowing the distance down to the ice gets you partway there.

You also need to know the aircraft’s altitude at the moment of the measurement. The same principle applies in orbit.

A precise record of where ICESat-2 was when it made a reading helps researchers determine the height of the surface below and compare it with measurements from later passes.

Those comparisons depend on a common set of coordinates called the terrestrial reference frame.

It gives scientists a consistent way to describe where objects are on and around Earth, even as the ground itself shifts.

Laser ranging helps maintain that system, so researchers using different instruments in different parts of the world can compare measurements of things like rising seas and moving tectonic plates.

There’s also a local complication for the team in Svalbard. The observatory sits next to a bird sanctuary where access is restricted during the summer breeding season.

The station can operate remotely when staff can’t get to the site, a capability NASA can carry over to future installations.

The Landsat image gives us one summer view of the fjord. Understanding how the landscape changes takes years of observations that can be lined up and compared.

From a patch of coast in that image, the Ny-Ålesund station helps make those comparisons possible, one pulse of light at a time.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin, using USGS Landsat data

#6372. Lake Mead’s water level ended October at its lowest point since it was first filled in 1937

Lake Mead ended September 2026 lower than at any month's end since 1937. The Park Service is planning for Temple Bar Marina before a drop expected in spring.

On October 22, 2026, the water behind Hoover Dam stood at 1,037.16 feet above sea level. According to the Bureau of Reclamation’s records, Lake Mead had not been that low since the spring of 1937, when the reservoir was still filling for the first time.

The previous low point of the drought came in July 2022, when the lake ended the month at 1,040.92 feet. This year it finished August, September and October below that mark.

Now the National Park Service (NPS) is preparing for what comes next. On November 20, officials announced that the NPS is developing a low-water strategy for Temple Bar Marina.

It lies on the Arizona side of Lake Mead National Recreation Area, and changes to marina operations are expected in early spring 2027.

At its current location, Temple Bar Marina needs a lake elevation of roughly 1,030 to 1,035 feet to keep running its marina and other water-based services, the park said.

According to the park’s November 20 announcement, Bureau of Reclamation projections show Lake Mead staying between 1,040 and 1,041 feet for the rest of 2026, then falling below 1,020 feet by May 2027.

The Park Service has secured $539,000 for the operations, logistics and visitor services needed to maintain lake access at the marina’s current location down to 1,020 feet as water levels fluctuate.

Below that threshold, the Park Service and the marina’s operator, LMNRA Guest Services, are preparing an orderly transition that includes removing or repositioning marina infrastructure.

“Lake Mead has a long history of adapting to changing conditions while keeping recreational opportunities available to the public,” said Ed Clark, the park’s acting superintendent.

The concessioner will contact affected vessel owners directly about what they may need to do, when, and what options they have. Owners remain responsible for safely removing or relocating their boats as conditions change.

Not everything at Temple Bar depends on the water line. The strategy also covers the land-based services, including lodging, dining and the trailer village, which the operator plans to keep running with reduced staff.

The park is still weighing options for maintaining boat launch access at Temple Bar, in line with its Sustainable Low Water Access Plan, and is asking people who use the area to check its website regularly for updates on the marina and access.

Temple Bar is one of five key locations covered by that plan, along with Hemenway Harbor, Callville Bay, Echo Bay and South Cove.

When it is full, Lake Mead reaches about 1,220 feet near the dam and holds 9.3 trillion gallons of water, according to NASA’s Earth Observatory. It last came close to full in the summers of 1983 and 1999.

Reclamation’s monthly records show how steep the drop has been. At the end of July 2000, the lake stood at 1,199.97 feet. At the end of September 2026, it was about 162 feet lower.

The pale bands visible along the shoreline in satellite images are mineral deposits on rock that used to be underwater when the reservoir was fuller. They are often called the “bathtub ring.”

Lake Mead is the largest reservoir in the United States. Most of its water comes from snowmelt in the Rocky Mountains, which flows down the Colorado River through Lake Powell and the Grand Canyon.

Only about 10% comes from local rain and groundwater each year, NASA says. Upstream, Lake Powell has fallen to its lowest level ever recorded.

The Colorado River system supplies water and electricity to roughly 40 million people, including the cities of Las Vegas, Phoenix, Los Angeles and San Diego, as well as 4 to 5 million acres of farmland in the Southwest, and the basin is also losing groundwater where scientists least expected.

In November, the lake rose slightly, from 1,038.85 feet at the end of October. By November 20 it stood at 1,041.36 feet, Reclamation’s daily records show.

The bigger question is what happens upstream. In its dry-scenario forecast published on November 16, Reclamation assumed that only 6.21 million acre-feet of water would flow into Lake Powell over the 2027 water year, 65% of average.

Reclamation describes that scenario as a dry condition that, statistically, would be exceeded 90% of the time, meaning inflows would likely be higher in about nine years out of 10.

Even under those assumptions, Lake Mead was projected to end 2026 at 1,040.19 feet.

The forecast predicts a steep drop in spring 2027. In the same scenario, the lake would fall to 1,032.41 feet by the end of March 2027 and to 1,016.93 feet by the end of May, below the 1,020-foot level down to which the park has funded lake access at the marina.

The Temple Bar strategy builds on the park’s ongoing efforts to keep motorized boating and lake access available on its Arizona side, and any boat launch option must be consistent with the 2023 Sustainable Low Water Access Plan and Environmental Assessment.

For now, the changes to marina operations are not expected until early spring 2027. What happens to the boats will depend on how far the lake falls in the spring.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s announcement on Temple Bar Marina and its page on the Sustainable Low Water Access Plan, the Bureau of Reclamation’s end-of-month elevations for Lake Mead, its daily reservoir levels and its November 2026 probable minimum 24-Month Study, and NASA Earth Observatory’s Lake Mead Keeps Dropping.

#6371. Young adults are turning to AI chatbots to ask about drugs and alcohol

About one in three young adults surveyed had asked an AI chatbot about drugs or alcohol, most often to find out what would happen if they used a substance.

About one in three young adults in a recent U.S. survey had turned to a chatbot with questions about drugs or alcohol. Most wanted to know what would happen if they used a substance.

Nearly all of the 995 young adults surveyed had used a chatbot like ChatGPT.

Of the 321 respondents who asked chatbots about substances, 155 did so at least monthly. Of those, 103 asked once a month, 39 once a week, and 13 daily or almost daily.

Mireia Triguero Roura, a postdoctoral researcher at the Rutgers Institute for Health, Health Care Policy and Aging Research, surveyed 995 Americans aged 18 to 29 in April 2026.

Pia Mauro, an associate professor at the Rutgers School of Public Health, was the co-author.

The respondents were recruited online, and the authors wrote that an online sample may make the habit look more common than it is.

The researchers said the finding concerned them, because the programs behind chatbots can easily reproduce false information.

“Using these tools can lead to misinformed or otherwise risky substance-use behavior among young people, who are the age group most affected by adverse effects of substance use,” Triguero Roura said.

A 2025 study in JAMA Network Open had found that about one in six young people used a chatbot for mental health advice. How many used one for drug and alcohol questions was unknown until this survey.

Among the 321 respondents who had asked a chatbot about substances, 92.8% wanted to know about the consequences of using one, such as the risks.

About half, 48.6%, asked for specifics about a substance, such as how much to take. Just over a third asked about addiction and related problems.

The chatbot users were also searching the old way. Of the 321, 298 had looked up substances on Google too, and across the whole survey 57.5% had done a substance-related Google search.

The chatbot was one more source, not a replacement.

The authors gave two reasons the numbers matter. Drugs or alcohol accounted for 25% of deaths among US young adults from 2018 to 2024, according to the federal mortality data they cited.

And news reports have described the overdose death of a young adult who had used a chatbot to learn about substance use.

Age made no measurable difference. Respondents aged 18 to 23 and those aged 24 to 29 were about equally likely to have asked, and so were students and non-students. Race and sex did make a difference.

Among the 139 Black respondents, 71 had asked a chatbot about substances, compared with 181 of the 607 white respondents.

Men were more likely than women to have asked about substances. Among men, 198 of 497 had asked, compared with 123 of 496 women.

Both gaps held after the researchers accounted for the other characteristics, including age and whether a respondent was a student.

Triguero Roura offered some possible reasons for the gaps, which the study didn’t test.

“The observed disparities in who chooses to use AI for drug-related inquiries could reflect differences in healthcare access, stigma, trust, and health information-seeking behaviors.”

Prolific, the platform the researchers used to recruit respondents, did not provide information on Hispanic origin, so the researchers could not report results separately for Hispanic young adults.

The 321 chatbot users also rated how helpful, reliable, and trustworthy they found chatbots on a scale of 1 to 5, once for everyday use and once for substance questions. Ratings were high for both.

Helpfulness scored higher for everyday use, 4.44 on the 5-point scale, than for substance questions, 4.12.

Trustworthiness was higher for substance questions, 3.66, than for everyday use, 3.51. Reliability was about the same for both.

So young adults found chatbots a little less helpful on drugs than on everything else, and a little more trustworthy. Anonymity may be part of the appeal, the authors wrote.

They also cited tests of chatbots on health questions that produced concerning results and noted that young adults could act on misinformation a chatbot repeats.

The researchers recruited respondents in April 2026 through Prolific, an online panel that verifies its participants and pays them for surveys. Each respondent earned 50 cents.

The sample was built to match the US young adult population, including roughly equal numbers of men and women.

The two age groups (18–23 and 24–29) were similar in size, and the racial breakdown was based on census survey figures.

Before asking about substances, the survey described what it meant by generative AI: chatbots or apps that mimic human conversation.

ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Meta AI, and Snap’s My AI were the examples given. Of the 995 people who passed the quality checks, 968 had used one at some point.

The 27 who hadn’t were counted as not having asked about substances. Five more respondents were dropped for failing the checks.

The researchers asked who used chatbots for substance questions, not what the chatbots told them.

Whether the answers were accurate, and what young adults did with them, is the open question, the authors wrote.

The sample is a limit too. People who sign up for online surveys may be more online, and more aware of AI, than young adults in general, so the one-in-three figure may run high.

The questions were adapted for this survey and hadn’t been tested before, and some answers may be inaccurate despite the quality checks.

Triguero Roura and Mauro wrote that the next studies should test how accurate chatbot answers about substances are, and how young adults interpret and act on them.

About a third of respondents had asked a chatbot about drugs or alcohol. What those chatbots told them remains an open question.

The full study was published in the journal JMIR Formative Research.

#6369. Petunias reveal an unexpected link between flower color and scent

Scientists studying petunias discovered that the same biological machinery responsible for flower color also shapes their scent.

Petunias use the same raw ingredient, an amino acid called phenylalanine, to make pigments and many of their scent compounds.

Researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem found that a protein called EOBV works with two proteins involved in pigmentation to regulate the flower’s scent.

When the researchers removed this protein, the flowers released more compounds associated with the smell of cloves and vanilla.

However, they released less methyl benzoate, normally the most abundant scent compound in these petunias.

Oded Skaliter and Alexander Vainstein ran all of it in petunias. The chemistry moved. Nobody has checked whether a nose, human or moth, can tell the difference.

Wild petunias have different ways of attracting pollinators. One species releases its fragrance at night to attract moths, another attracts bees with purple flowers, and a third uses red flowers to attract hummingbirds.

Petunia pigment is run by a committee of three, known to biologists as the MBW complex.

Two of these proteins, AN1 and AN11, remain the same. The third can be any one of several proteins belonging to a family called MYB, and its identity determines which genes the group controls.

Skaliter and his colleagues examined when AN1 and AN11 were most active.

Activity peaked as the flowers opened and remained high for another two days, around the same time that scent production reached its peak.

Then they knocked each gene down, one at a time, with a plant virus. Air from around the petals went into the analyzer.

Both treatments increased the release of eugenol and vanillin. The amount of methyl benzoate roughly doubled.

Rather than helping the flowers produce more fragrance, the pigment proteins appeared to hold scent production back.

The researchers suspected that the missing piece of the puzzle was the third protein in the group.

Six MYB proteins were already in the frame here, all of them previously linked to petunia fragrance.

Each went up against AN1 and AN11 in yeast cells that change color when two proteins bind. EOBV was the only hit.

The team repeated the experiment in living plant tissue. This time, they used a system that produces betalain, the red pigment found in beets, when proteins interact.

Leaves of a tobacco relative turned red when they received both AN1 and EOBV. Leaves that received AN1 alone produced a weaker color signal.

The strongest red color appeared when all three proteins were present. Removing any one of them greatly reduced pigment production in the test.

AN11 and EOBV would not bind each other. AN1 had to stand between them.

The researchers also found very little EOBV gene activity outside the petals. Within the petals, activity was about 1.8 times higher in the upper surface layer, through which fragrance escapes.

Previous work from the same laboratory found that a gene responsible for giving petals their identity also activates scent production.

The next step was to remove EOBV completely. A virus carried CRISPR gene-editing tools into petunia tissue, and the team recovered three groups of edited plants.

In one group, the instructions for starting the protein were gone, along with the first 42 amino acids. Production in the other two stopped after 58 and 91 amino acids.

The edited plants still looked and flowered like the originals.

Two-day-old flowers then went into sealed jars, two flowers to a jar, and whatever they gave off over the next 24 hours was trapped and measured.

Without a working version of EOBV, the flowers released more eugenol, both forms of isoeugenol and vanillin. These compounds give cloves and vanilla their familiar aromas.

However, the flowers released less of almost every other scent compound, including methyl benzoate. The total amount of fragrance released also fell.

The team then ground up petals to measure how much of each compound remained inside. The clove and vanilla compounds had increased there, too.

The petals contained similar amounts of methyl benzoate and several other scent compounds even though the edited flowers released less of them.

A repressor has to act on something, so the next question was which genes EOBV holds down. Gene activity was compared between edited and unedited flowers.

Most showed little difference. However, two genes, known as C4H2 and ADT3, became more active after the researchers removed EOBV.

C4H2 controls the carbon supply to the branch that produces eugenol, isoeugenol and vanillin.

The rise in C4H2 gene activity may help explain why the edited flowers made more eugenol, isoeugenol, and vanillin.

The team then tested that link directly. They connected the region of DNA that controls C4H2 activity to a system that produces red pigment.

Petals that received EOBV showed no visible red color. Petals without the additional EOBV produced more than twice as much pigment.

Two other fragrance genes, PAAS and BSMT, became less active in the edited flowers. Since EOBV does not appear to bind directly to the regions controlling these genes, the changes were probably indirect.

Researchers found a similar pattern in 2011 when they reduced the activity of another petunia gene called PhMYB4. PhMYB4 and EOBV are about 80% identical. Genetic testing confirmed that PhMYB4 itself had not been edited.

EOBV becomes more active when petunias grow in warmer conditions. The researchers wanted to see whether removing it could protect flowers from heat.

They grew the plants in a greenhouse for a month before moving them into two rooms. The cooler room had temperatures of 72°F (22°C) during the day and 61°F (16°C) at night. The warmer room reached 82°F (28°C) and 72°F (22°C), respectively.

After measuring 38 flowers, the team found that unedited flowers became 12% narrower in warmer conditions. Edited flowers shrank by only 6%.

Heat also reduced the amount of scent released by unedited flowers, mainly due to lower emissions of benzaldehyde and methyl benzoate. Edited flowers maintained their overall scent output.

Meanwhile, PhEXP1, a gene that helps petal cells expand, became less active in both groups by similar amounts.

Heat-shrunk petunia flowers were traced to slower cell division in a 2021 study, a step this team did not measure.

More vanilla and clove compounds might sound appealing, but would these petunias actually smell better?

Nobody has asked people to smell the edited flowers. The researchers haven’t tested pollinators either.

Removing EOBV also has limits. In purple varieties, reducing EOBV activity left pigment levels unchanged.

EOBV belongs to the color machinery without fixing the shade of purple itself.

The team also crossed the edited plants with petunias lacking EVER, another scent regulator. Those flowers did not outperform either parent. The authors suggest limited carbon, or a limited capacity to release scent.

The authors also disclosed a commercial interest. Skaliter and Vainstein are chief technology officer and chief scientific officer at CapsiBreed, which uses gene editing in hot and sweet peppers. Peppers and petunias are relatives.

One obvious next experiment is to switch EOBV off in plants that are already missing AN1 or AN11.

The team also wants to know whether other flowering plants are wired this way. And growers will want an answer to a blunter question: does a reshuffled scent give them flowers that anyone wants to buy?

The full study was published in the journal Plant Physiology.
