#6368. Sitting behind the wheel may do something unusual to your heart rate

Driving keeps the heart above its resting rate for longer, even when the body remains seated and inactive.

Sitting behind the wheel is usually treated as no different from sitting anywhere else. Heart-rate readings that were collected for a week from 57 young adults in Texas now suggest otherwise.

During the time these people spent driving, their heart rates remained above resting level almost throughout. A return to resting level was recorded about half as often as during other inactive hours.

Their hearts were not found to beat faster in the car than during those other hours. The resting pace was simply reached less often while a person was driving.

The study was designed and supervised by Ioannis Pavlidis who is a computer science professor at the University of Houston.

Colleagues from the same university and from the Texas A&M Transportation Institute worked with him.

Pavlidis said that a driver has to keep watching the road and deciding what to do next.

“The body may be sitting, but the mind is working,” he said. According to him, it is in the heart rate that this mental work can be seen.

What the study isn’t able to show is that driving itself kept anyone’s heart rate up. The comparison that was made was between time spent driving and other inactive time in one week.

There are more differences between these two kinds of time than the car alone.

Posture and caffeine are on the list of them that the authors gave and so are passengers. How urgently a driver needed to arrive is on that list as well.

The group consisted of 30 men and 27 women with an average age of about 26. Most of them were office workers.

A personal iPhone and Apple Watch were used by each participant from Monday through Sunday.

Every car was fitted with a small plug-in device by which each period of driving could be recorded. The watch was the source of the heart rate readings to which weather and traffic conditions were matched.

The rest of each day was labeled with the help of activity data from the phone and the watch. Any recorded minute in which a person was neither driving nor physically active was taken into the comparison.

Such minutes may have been spent at work or at home or somewhere else entirely.

The batteries of the iPhone and Apple Watch had usually run out by early evening. It is for this reason that the recordings cover daytime hours alone.

It was Pavlidis’ group at the Affective and Data Computing Laboratory that averaged the readings minute by minute. The recordings that resulted came to 177,318 minutes which is close to 3,000 hours.

No heart-rate reading existed for 13.6% of the driving minutes or for 3.5% of other inactive minutes. Neither speed nor traffic was found to be linked to the readings that were missing.

Driving took up about a tenth of that time. There were 973 trips in total and half of them were over within 15 minutes. A crash or a traffic ticket was generally not part of these drives.

Before any single minute could be judged, the team had to know each person’s resting heart rate.

An estimate of it is produced by the Apple Watch once a day. These daily estimates were averaged by the team across the whole week.

While a person was driving, their heart rate was above their own resting level 93.7% of the time on average. The figure for other inactive time was 81.3%.

Yet a higher heart rate in the car was not what the Houston team found. During driving, it averaged 11.2 beats per minute above resting level. The average for other inactive time was 11.5 beats above resting level.

A gap as small as that could have come up by chance.

Where driving did differ was in how little the heart rate varied. Its typical spread was 7.98 beats per minute during driving and 12.40 beats during other inactive time.

Heart rates dropped to resting level 2.46 times per hour during other inactive time and 1.31 times per hour while driving.

On weekdays, the two shares of time above resting level were 93.8% and 82.1%.

Weekends showed the same pattern, although people then spend their hours outside the car differently.

According to Pavlidis, a workout also raises heart rate, but the body becomes fitter as a result of it. From the time that is spent behind the wheel, no benefit of that kind is gained.

Yasmine Bouzid and the other authors also examined what a higher or lower heart rate was tied to.

During driving, there were two things that stood out from the rest. Time of day was the first since heart rates were higher in drives after noon than in the morning.

The second was the amount by which the driver’s wrist had turned in the minute before. The gyroscope of the Apple Watch supplied this measure which was treated as a sign of steering.

Away from the car, the list that was found was a broader one. On it were age and sex along with time of day and the Big Five personality trait of openness.

For this, the authors offered one reason which they regarded as possible. Driving is a single task whose demands remain fairly steady from one minute to the next.

Many different situations are covered by the inactive time that is spent away from the car.

Because a drive is repeated day after day, an example using anxiety was worked through by the team.

The volunteers had filled out the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, which scores a tendency to feel anxious from 20 to 80. The lowest score that was found in this group was 20 while the highest was 61.

Over every recorded minute of driving, the team’s heart-rate model was then run twice. A score of 20 was given to every driver in the first of these runs. In the second run, it was a score of 61 that every driver was given.

The heart rate that the model predicted with the score of 61 was higher by 0.99 beats per minute.

What the Houston team then did was to count such beats over a whole year. For a person who drives eight hours a day, the model projected about 173,000 extra heartbeats.

It came to roughly 11,000 extra heartbeats when the same was done for a 30-minute daily drive.

It was only as illustrations that these totals were described by Pavlidis and his coauthors. What they show is how a small difference accumulates, and not what anyone’s risk of heart disease is.

There were only young adults from Texas among the 57 volunteers, and none was followed for more than a week. Older drivers, professional drivers, or people with heart disease may not show the results that were found here.

It will take years of following drivers before the health side of this can be judged. Only then can it be learned whether more time above resting heart rate predicts heart problems.

Pavlidis said that driving is something many people can’t do without. What his lab in Houston wants to find out is how the same trips could be made less demanding.

The Texas A&M Transportation Institute, where study co-author Michael Manser works, is supporting the lab through 2027.

The people who are to be studied next include long-distance commuters and those who drive for a living.

Rideshare drivers are an example of the latter. The groups are meant to be bigger, more varied, and followed for longer.

There is one more question that self-driving cars from Waymo and Tesla have raised for the lab. What does a rider’s heart rate do when it is the vehicle that handles the driving?

The full study was published in the journal npj Digital Public Health.

#6367. A con man claimed his secret gold mine was paying for a $2 million castle in Death Valley, but the mine never existed

A man nicknamed "Death Valley Scotty" said his gold mine paid for Scotty's Castle. That wasn't true. Here's what really happened.

In the 1920s, reporters who made the trip to a remote canyon in northern Death Valley found a Spanish-style mansion rising out of the desert.

Walter Scott, better known as “Death Valley Scotty,” had an explanation for it. He was building the two million dollar home, he said, with profits from his secret gold mine.

There was no mine. The house belonged to Albert Mussey Johnson, a Chicago insurance millionaire who had been sending Scotty money for years, according to the National Park Service.

When reporters asked Johnson about it, he agreed that Scotty owned the place and described himself simply as “Scotty’s banker.”

A century later, the estate still carries the con man’s name. But Scotty’s Castle has been closed to regular visits since a flash flood in October 2015, and in October 2026 the park said the earliest it could fully reopen is November 2028.

Scott was born in Kentucky in 1872. He ran away as a boy to join two of his brothers in Nevada, worked at the Harmony Borax Works and rode in Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West Show, according to the park.

After leaving the show in 1902, he turned to gold prospecting and convinced several wealthy businessmen that he had a claim to a fabulous gold mine in Death Valley.

Scott offered to split the profits if they first put up money to extract the ore. When no gold arrived, most of his investors decided they had been conned and backed out.

In July 1905, Scotty traveled by train to Chicago with a roll of money, falsely claiming to have struck it rich in a Death Valley mine. The trip broke the travel time record and opened doors among the wealthy elite.

According to the park’s biography of Johnson, he had already invested in Scotty’s mine in 1904, and he kept sending money even after the person he sent to check on Scott reported that there was no gold mine.

In 1906, Johnson tried to visit the mine himself. On the way into the valley, his party was attacked in what became known as the Battle of Wingate Pass, and Scotty’s brother Warner was shot. The park describes Scotty as a flamboyant con artist and showman.

When Johnson finally made it to Death Valley, Scotty took him on a grueling trek by horseback, apparently expecting the desert to be too much for him.

Johnson had been badly injured in a train accident in his youth. Instead, he stayed nearly a month, and his health improved dramatically in the dry, sunny climate.

He never saw the mine and was almost certainly being swindled, the park says, but he did not seem to mind. The two men became lifelong friends.

Johnson went on to buy land in spring-fed Grapevine Canyon, about 3,000 feet above sea level, eventually owning 1,500 acres.

His wife, Bessie, suggested building something more comfortable than the canvas tents they had been using, so they could “get away from the rattlesnakes and scorpions.”

Work on what they called Death Valley Ranch began in the 1920s, and the garage built in 1922 served as the workshop for the construction.

Scotty, who recognized a good story, told everyone the house was his. Even the concrete posts along the property’s fence were stamped with an “S” for Scotty and a “J” for Johnson, the true owner.

Construction stopped in 1931, when Johnson discovered that, because of a surveying error, he had been building on federal land.

The Great Depression was beginning to take hold, and the work never resumed. The castle was left incomplete, and its swimming pool was never finished.

Johnson died in 1948 and left most of his fortune and property to the Gospel Foundation, which he had founded two years earlier.

Scotty had the right to live at the castle for the rest of his life. He died in January 1954. Johnson had hoped the National Park Service would one day buy the property, and in 1970 it did.

For decades, rangers in period costume led tours through the house and told the story of the Johnsons and their friend.

On the night of October 18, 2015, Scotty’s Castle received 2 3/4 inches of rain, about a year’s worth, in five hours, after a half-inch the day before.

A flash flood of mud and rocks poured down Grapevine Canyon at an estimated 3,200 cubic feet per second, according to the park. On steep slopes like these, heavy rain can trigger flash floods faster than expected.

Rangers sheltered with about 20 stranded visitors on the rim of Ubehebe Crater that night, and one ranger watched power poles and metal dumpsters float out of the canyon. Nobody was hurt.

The main house mostly escaped the flood. The historic garage, which served as the visitor center, did not. The water broke through its windows, doors and walls and left four feet of mud and rocks inside.

The unfinished pool filled many feet deep with mud and debris, and most of the 8-mile road through the canyon was destroyed.

Repairs were under way in April 2021 when contractors arrived one morning to find the garage on fire, with flames spreading to the neighboring Longshed. The garage was destroyed.

A state investigation found the fire started inside the building but could not determine a cause and found no evidence of arson.

The park has given two figures for how far the garage repairs had gone, 37% in a June 2021 release and 60% on its recovery page. One of the upgrades being installed was fire sprinklers.

In 2019, the park expected to reopen the castle in October 2021. After the fire, the target moved to 2023. It is now November 2028 at the earliest.

The park lists funding and staffing problems, legal reviews to protect historic and natural features, contracting issues, unforeseen conditions, the pandemic, more flooding and the fire.

The repairs cost about $71 million, split into separate projects so they could be funded from different sources.

Some of the work is done. New berms and flood walls finished in January 2023 protected the historic district when the remnants of Hurricane Hilary hit the park that August. The road through the canyon has been rebuilt.

The next phase, expected to start in 2027, covers the parking lot, the Longshed and the historic Gas Tank House, which will become a small visitor contact station in place of the burned garage.

After that, curators will return the furnishings and museum collections to the house before interior tours can resume.

Until then, the only way in is a guided tour. This season, rangers and guides from the Death Valley Natural History Association are leading exterior tours of the grounds on most Saturdays and Sundays through April 17.

Tickets are sold through the association. Bonnie Clare Road, the 8-mile route through Grapevine Canyon, remains closed to the public, including pedestrians.

Once the castle is fully reopened, the park plans to open it each year from late fall through early spring.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s October 2026 announcement on Scotty’s Castle tours, its pages on the Scotty’s Castle flood and recovery, building the castle, Death Valley Scotty, Albert Mussey Johnson and the showmen of Death Valley tourism, and its releases on the 2021 fire, the fire investigation and the repairs four years after the flood.

#6366. Rand Paul chooses ranking member slot at Senate HELP

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., leaves the Senate Republicans’ lunch in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday he plans to serve as the top Republican on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul currently chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.

The move fit in with Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s bid to use her seniority to succeed Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, as top Republican on the Appropriations panel. If Paul did not go to the top spot on HELP, Murkowski, R-Alaska, would be next in line for that committee in the next Congress.

Murkowski is second in seniority on Appropriations to Collins, who was defeated for reelection. But she faces a potential challenge from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., who is next in line behind her.

Paul said in a press release that he plans to bring the same approach to the HELP Committee as he did as chairman of Homeland, where he said he “challenged entrenched bureaucracies, forced federal officials to answer for their actions, and pulled back the curtain on what Washington tried to keep hidden.”

He cited calling Dr. Anthony Fauci before the committee to probe the former federal health official’s role in pandemic-related shutdowns and the origin of the COVID-19 virus, and releasing thousands of pages of pandemic-related documents. The panel voted in August to hold Fauci in criminal contempt of Congress for declining to answer questions about the pandemic during a highly charged hearing.

Related: Fauci could face criminal contempt charge following panel vote

Paul, an ophthalmologist, said at HELP he will “stand against efforts to put Washington between Americans and their doctors, their children’s schools, and their paychecks.” He predicted “a rush toward socialism unlike anything we have seen” when the Democrat-controlled Congress convenes in January.

Lankford, in a separate statement, confirmed his interest in becoming the ranking member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. In many areas, he said, the panel can work in a bipartisan manner, and over the past decade he “worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence.”

But he added that his job also would be to “push back on a [Democratic] majority that goes too far . . . Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.”

Lankford said he would work together with the likely committee chair, Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., “when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.”

#6365. The second most common element in the universe is actually running out here on Earth

Most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space. In 1868, astronomers studying a total solar eclipse spotted a mysterious…

Most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space. In 1868, astronomers studying a total solar eclipse spotted a mysterious yellow band in the Sun’s light spectrum that did not match any known element.

The British scientist Norman Lockyer named the mystery substance helium after Helios, the Greek god of the Sun, as recounted by the American Physical Society.

Humanity had identified an element in starlight 93 million miles (150 million kilometers) away before anyone held a sample of it.

Confirmation took decades. The Scottish chemist William Ramsay finally isolated terrestrial helium in 1895, releasing it from a uranium-bearing mineral nearly 27 years after Lockyer first saw its signature.

That long delay hints at the problem now reshaping hospitals and laboratories. Helium is the second-most-abundant element in the universe, yet it is genuinely rare on Earth.

The contradiction comes down to gravity. Helium is so light that it drifts upward, escapes the atmosphere, and is lost to space forever. Our Moon even collects traces of the gases our planet sheds. The cosmic abundance simply never settled here.

The helium we use does not come from the Big Bang reservoir that fills the cosmos. It forms underground, atom by atom, as radioactive uranium and thorium decay within the crust.

Those elements decay on almost unimaginable timescales. Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years and thorium-232 closer to 14 billion years, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Each decay releases the alpha particles that become helium.

The same slow chemistry that shaped Earth’s crust over billions of years also governs its helium. No factory can shortcut that process, which is why no large-scale method exists to manufacture the gas artificially.

This is the deeper reason the current squeeze matters. A shortfall in most materials invites more mining or more production. A helium shortfall invites neither, because the planet replenishes its supply only as fast as atoms decay.

Producers extract helium as a trace component of natural gas, and only deposits with high enough concentrations are worth tapping. That narrow geology leaves the market exposed to plant shutdowns and trade disruptions.

The strain is already visible. Hospitals consume roughly a third of the world’s helium to cool the superconducting magnets in MRI scanners, and analysts expect global demand to double by 2035 as semiconductor and electric-vehicle manufacturing expand.

The hunt for fresh supply is reaching parts of the world that never produced helium before. In Tanzania, the Southern Rukwa project finalized its mining agreements in May 2026, positioning the country to extract helium at a commercial scale. Qatar has also moved to bring new capacity online.

Policy decisions have added uncertainty. The United States sold its Federal Helium System, once the planet’s largest single source, to the industrial gas company Messer in June 2024, ending nearly a century of public stewardship, the U.S. Bureau of Land Management confirmed.

Newer MRI machines now seal and recirculate their helium, and many labs capture and re-liquefy every drop they can. These measures buy time, much as a simple scan can buy a patient time. Whether they arrive fast enough is the open question.

There is a quiet symmetry to the helium story. We discovered it by looking up at a star, much as a meteorite can reveal a vanished world, and we may yet preserve it by looking down into the rocks that hoard it.

For now, the element that fills birthday balloons remains one of the most strategically important substances on the planet. It reminds us that some of Earth’s rarest things are those we first noticed in the heavens.

The full study was published in the journal Physics Today.

#6364. Crews tearing up a 1950s parking lot at Dinosaur National Monument hit fossils, but the real find was a dinosaur tail with nine vertebrae

Under a Dinosaur National Monument parking lot, a paleontologist found a likely Diplodocus tail with nine vertebrae in the first dig there since 1924.

In September 2025, road crews at Dinosaur National Monument in Utah peeled back the asphalt outside the Quarry Exhibit Hall, the most popular stop in the park. They were there to rebuild a parking lot. The first scoop of the backhoe brought up pieces of fossil bone.

Over the next five weeks, the job turned into a dinosaur dig.

Park paleontologist ReBecca Hunt-Foster and her assistant followed a trail of bones through the rock until they had uncovered nine tail vertebrae and the leg and arm bones of a long-necked dinosaur, most likely Diplodocus.

Its relatives still turn up in surprising places, including the first Diplodocus ever found outside North America.

It was the first fossil excavation in that part of the historic Carnegie Quarry since 1924, the National Park Service said. In an account published this fall, Hunt-Foster described how the last bones of the tail were lying right against the old asphalt.

The spot has a long history. On August 17, 1909, Earl Douglass, a paleontologist from the Carnegie Museum in Pittsburgh, spotted eight dinosaur tailbones sticking out of a sandstone ledge in the Utah desert. “It was a beautiful sight,” he wrote in his diary.

His crews spent the next 13 years digging there and collected more than 317 metric tons of fossils and rock between 1909 and 1922, according to Hunt-Foster, much of it shipped back to Pittsburgh.

The Smithsonian dug on the east side of the quarry in 1923, and the University of Utah in 1924. In 1915, President Woodrow Wilson set aside the quarry and 80 acres around it as Dinosaur National Monument.

All that digging produced a lot of waste rock. It was dumped off the eastern side of the quarry, and in the 1930s, New Deal work crews cleared more debris while improving the road.

Those tailing piles later became the parking lot for the Quarry Exhibit Hall, which opened in 1958 around a wall of rock where visitors can see about 1,500 dinosaur fossils still in place.

In May 2025, the park was due to begin an $11.2 million project to upgrade roads, parking areas and overlooks along the route to the Quarry Exhibit Hall.

Because the work crossed fossil-bearing rock, the park brought on a seasonal paleontological assistant, Rudolph Hummel, to watch the construction.

The biggest worry was the parking lot. Fossils overlooked by the early excavators, or judged not worth keeping, could be sitting in the old tailings. The bone-bearing sandstone itself might also turn up.

The road and the exhibit hall closed from September 8 to late October 2025. Monitoring in the parking lot began on September 10, after the asphalt cap came off.

On September 11, the team found the first identifiable bone, a vertebra from a meat-eating dinosaur, likely Allosaurus. Smaller finds followed every day as the crew dug down five feet. Construction sites have a way of turning up fossils, as a Los Angeles project showed.

The construction workers got caught up in it too. Many of them jumped in to search for fossils by hand rather than by backhoe alone, Hunt-Foster wrote, and one worker spent two days power-washing a section of the sandstone so it could be studied.

On September 16, after that washing was done, Hunt-Foster was documenting the exposed sandstone when she spotted a fossil bone in its cross section.

It turned out to be a large limb bone plunging down into the rock. Construction in that corner of the lot was paused.

After a week of digging, the pair found a tail vertebra lying over the long bone, which they identified as a sauropod tibia. Then a second vertebra appeared, and a third, all still connected. Hummel followed them east while Hunt-Foster worked west.

Six more tail vertebrae turned up, along with the bones of the lower arm. By then, the team had concluded that the tail likely belonged to Diplodocus, the most abundant dinosaur in the Carnegie Quarry.

They also found a partial turtle, plenty of freshwater clams and carbonized wood lying directly under the skeleton.

By September 26, the team had reached the end of the tail. The vertebrae grew smaller toward the east, and the last one was missing its back half, cleanly sheared off and tilted up toward the old surface.

Hunt-Foster and Hummel suspect that the tip of the tail, if it was preserved at all, was plowed off when the road was first built in the late 1950s. Several of the last vertebrae were in direct contact with the asphalt from the lot’s first paving.

Photos from the visitor center’s opening on June 1, 1958, show the lot was still gravel, and it does not appear to have been paved until around 1959, she wrote.

All of this happened while the new parking lot was being built around the dig. Dump trucks full of fill rolled past and rollers packed down the ground around them. “In a short amount of time, we were sitting in a deep trench surrounded by a fresh parking lot,” Hunt-Foster wrote.

Volunteers, a Utah Conservation Corps crew, park coworkers and construction staff helped wrap the bones in protective field jackets. The first small jacket came out on October 13. On October 17, the construction crew’s backhoe operator lifted out the rest.

In all, about 3,000 pounds of fossils and rock came out of the 2025 dig. The bones are now being cleaned and studied at the Utah Field House of Natural History State Park Museum in Vernal, Utah.

Visitors can watch the work in the museum’s fossil preparation lab. Some fossils from the excavation are also on display at the Quarry Exhibit Hall.

The parking lot is finished, and the Quarry Exhibit Hall is open daily except on Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day.

The story is not over. Hunt-Foster says a second part of her account will cover continued excavation work in 2026 and additional discoveries.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s January 2026 announcement of the excavation, ReBecca Hunt-Foster’s article The Parking Lot Sauropod of Dinosaur National Monument: Part 1 in Park Paleontology News, and the park’s pages on Earl Douglass and the historic Carnegie Quarry.

#6363. Possible new dwarf planet that is roughly 930 miles wide had gone unnoticed in telescope images since 2016

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory discovered 2026 ED138, a distant dwarf planet candidate beyond Neptune whose size and shape remain unconfirmed.

A distant object named 2026 ED138 may be a dwarf planet between 370 and 930 miles (600 and 1,500 kilometers) wide, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory announced on October 27, 2026.

Archival images show that another instrument, the Dark Energy Camera, had recorded it since February 25, 2016, without anyone noticing.

The object remains a candidate because its size has been estimated, not measured.

Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, found the object on the evening of October 13. He was running Rubin data collected earlier in 2026 through a search code developed with colleague Kevin Napier.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said.

“Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong,” he added.

The code first detected a cluster of ten observations on eight nights. Mario Jurić, Rubin’s solar system lead scientist at the University of Washington, then found 20 more in Rubin’s catalogs and images.

In all, the observatory’s telescope saw the object 30 times on 20 nights between March 4 and July 11. The results were presented at a planetary science meeting in Spokane, Washington.

“It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years,” Jurić said.

The object is currently about 46 astronomical units from the Sun, or roughly 4.3 billion miles (6.9 billion kilometers). Pluto averages 39 of those units, each equal to Earth’s distance from the Sun, by NASA‘s figures.

Its orbit, which comes no closer to the Sun than about 37 astronomical units, is tilted almost 25 degrees from the solar system’s plane. The announcement suggests that gravitational interactions with Neptune disturbed the object’s original path.

Earlier surveys missed 2026 ED138 because it lies far south and near the crowded regions of the Galactic plane, the discovery paper states. In April, Rubin had already submitted observations of more than 11,000 new asteroids.

Given the orbit computed from Rubin data alone, an archive search service returned older candidate detections. The object appears in 45 Dark Energy Camera exposures on 14 nights, the last on April 7, 2023.

“Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look,” Jurić explained.

A century-long archival search, posted on November 2 and not yet peer-reviewed, pushes the record back further. It reports the object on 12 photographic plates taken between 1954 and 2000, plus a marginal detection on a 1937 plate.

The diameter is calculated from the object’s brightness and an assumed albedo, the fraction of sunlight its surface reflects. That albedo has not been measured.

The upper end of the announced range requires a very dark surface, one that reflects only four percent of the light. A diameter between 380 and 600 miles (612 and 968 kilometers) is more probable, by the discoverers’ own assessment.

Pluto, Eris and Makemake, whose surfaces are rich in methane ice, reflect about 60 to 90 percent of sunlight. So bright a surface is considered less likely for 2026 ED138, although its composition is still unknown.

“Thermal photometry or a stellar occultation is needed to decide between these sizes,” the authors wrote. An occultation occurs when an object passes in front of a star and briefly blocks its light.

The archival study predicts 15 such events between 2027 and 2030, six of them over populated land. It also reports a tentative rotation signal with a period of 10.4 hours.

By intrinsic brightness, the object ranks ninth or tenth among known bodies beyond Neptune, depending on which measurements are compared.

Under the 2006 definition of the International Astronomical Union (IAU), a dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is not a satellite. Its own gravity must pull it into a nearly round shape, and it has not cleared the neighborhood around its orbit.

The IAU has so far recognized five: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake and Eris. “If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds,” Holman said.

Icy bodies as large as 2026 ED138 are expected to be round, the Rubin release states. Whether this one is compact and round is less certain, its discoverers cautioned in their paper.

A 2019 study of a distant binary suggested that objects 250 to 620 miles (400 to 1,000 kilometers) wide mark a transition.

Smaller bodies stay porous, while larger ones have collapsed their internal voids under much higher pressures and temperatures.

The discovery team estimates that about three more objects this bright, and probably more, remain undiscovered away from the Galactic plane. Rubin’s ten-year survey of the southern sky began in June 2026.

The study is available as a preprint on arXiv.

An unusual pair of seated figurines was discovered in a Stone Age grave in Romania in the 1950s.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Two Stone Age figurines ‪—‬ the Thinker and the Seated Woman ‪—‬ were discovered in a prehistoric cemetery in Romania.

In 1956, archaeologists unearthed two unique figurines from one grave while excavating a Stone Age cemetery in southeast Romania. The unusual figurines — known as the Thinkers of Cernavodă or the Thinker and the Seated Woman — were made by people from the Hamangia culture and may be linked to ancient astronomical beliefs.

The Thinkers of Cernavodă are in the collection of the National Museum of Romanian History and are a key part of the country's cultural heritage. They were crafted from fired clay and measure about 4.5 inches (11.5 centimeters) tall. The two figurines may represent a man (the Thinker) and a woman (the Seated Woman), according to the museum.

The Thinker sits on a low, four-legged stool. He bends forward slightly, rounding his back and neck, and his arms are bent. He rests his elbows on his knees and his head in his hands. This pose gives him a meditative quality, according to the museum, which is why he has been named after Auguste Rodin's famous 1904 bronze sculpture. The Seated Woman also has a long, bent neck and a small face. She has prominent hips, thighs and breasts. Her right leg is bent, and her hands rest on her knee.

The figurines are about 7,000 years old and were made by the Hamangia people, a Late Neolithic culture that stretched from the Danube River to the Black Sea. According to archaeologist Dumitru Berciu, who excavated the Cernavodă cemetery, the Hamangia culture lasted from about 5200 to 4500 B.C. The people focused primarily on sheep and goat herding, and they built defensive hilltop settlements. They also crafted spiral-decorated pottery and human-shaped figurines. But while Berciu found dozens of male and female figurines in the Cernavodă cemetery, he noted that both Thinkers were unusual for being depicted seated rather than standing.

The specific meaning of the Thinkers is unclear. Berciu suggested that the figurines were somewhat stylized, rather than realistic, because they served a magical or religious purpose. Since solar worship was common among later Bronze Age groups in Europe — as evidenced by artifacts like the Nebra sky disc from Germany and an ornate sun chariot from Denmark — Berciu interpreted the figurines as possibly connected to sun worship.

But the National Museum of Romanian History has suggested that the two figurines may have been made specifically as a pair, representing the complementary principles of masculine and feminine natures or a Neolithic family unit. Another interpretation is that the sculptures depict a pair of mourners who were buried with the deceased.

While the original meaning of the 7,000-year-old sculptures remains a mystery, people continue to be drawn to the contemplative pair, and the male Thinker figures prominently today in the logo of the National Museum of Romanian History.

#6361. Most of the world’s lost glacier ice comes from a tiny minority of glaciers

A census of 216,502 glaciers finds the 3 percent that end in lakes, seas or ice shelves drive most glacier ice loss, and lakes speed it up most.

Outside of Earth’s two massive ice sheets, there are roughly 216,500 glaciers, and 97 percent of them end on bare rock. Surprisingly, however, these land-based glaciers are not where most of the world’s melting ice is coming from.

The other 3 percent end in a lake, the ocean, or a floating ice shelf. They are the ones shedding more than half of all the glacier ice lost between 2000 and 2019.

Those numbers come from a new global census of where glaciers end. Glaciers that end in lakes stood out most. Relative to their size, they lost ice about 57 percent faster than glaciers ending on land. The researchers don’t yet know why.

Joe Mallalieu did the work at the University of Birmingham and is now at the University of Leeds, with Nicholas Barrand of Birmingham among the co-authors.

In an interview with Earth.com, Mallalieu said the lake result was a surprise.

“What surprised us most was how much faster glaciers ending in lakes lose ice than those ending in the ocean, relative to their size,” he said.

The team classified all 216,502 glaciers in a standard global inventory by what their fronts touch: land, a lake, the sea, or an ice shelf.

Earlier inventories had flagged lake-ending glaciers in only three of the world’s 19 glacier regions. The team found the rest by matching glacier outlines against a satellite map of glacial lakes built from more than 250,000 Landsat scenes.

Then they combined that classification with existing global records of each glacier’s size, ice thickness, slope, flow speed and ice loss, plus the local climate. The full classification is public on Zenodo.

Lake-ending glaciers turned up in every one of the 19 regions. In Iceland, 65 percent of the glacier area drains to a lake, and in the southern Andes almost 40 percent does. Glaciers ending in the sea cluster in the Arctic and around Antarctica.

Glaciers that end in lakes or the sea tend to be far bigger than those ending on land. The typical lake-ending glacier covered about eight times the area of a typical land-ending one.

It was also roughly twice as thick, about 200 feet (61 meters) against 100 feet (31 meters).

Size alone explained a lot of the ice loss but not all of it. For its size, the typical lake-ending glacier lost ice equal to a layer of water about 1.6 feet (0.49 meters) deep each year.

That is roughly double the rate at land-ending and ocean-ending glaciers.

After the team accounted for climate, elevation, slope, thickness and other factors, the gap held. Lake-ending glaciers lost about 57 percent more ice for their size than land-ending ones, and they flowed about 10 percent faster.

Ocean-ending glaciers flowed 44 percent faster than land-ending ones, yet their ice loss for their size was no higher, the authors wrote.

Lake water can remove ice from a glacier’s front in several ways. It melts the ice below the waterline, and the undercut front breaks off as icebergs.

It can also lift the front until it floats and breaks, or seep beneath the ice and reduce the friction holding it back.

Any of those would remove ice faster than melting on bare rock does. But the lake-ending glaciers in the census were also larger and flatter at their lower ends than land-ending ones.

That shape alone can slow a glacier’s adjustment to warming and keep it losing ice for longer, the authors wrote.

Mallalieu told Earth.com that even the climate difference doesn’t account for it. “And it’s not just because they tend to be in warmer, wetter places: the difference holds even when we take climate into account,” he said.

Barrand said the census only became possible recently. “The last decade has seen a huge increase in the global glacier and climate data available to researchers. Bringing these datasets together lets us compare how glaciers in different settings are behaving,” he said.

The categories themselves are moving. Glacial lakes grew by more than 50 percent in number and area between 1990 and 2018, according to a satellite survey in Nature Climate Change.

Many glaciers that once ended on land now end in water. Across the Arctic, meanwhile, glaciers that reached the sea are retreating onto land.

Asked by Earth.com what happens to those glaciers next, Mallalieu said the two switches should have opposite effects.

Glaciers pulling back onto land are likely to slow down markedly. Glaciers newly ending in lakes are likely to speed up slightly and lose ice much faster for their size.

In the long run, he said, many lake-ending glaciers will retreat out of their lakes and end on land again. That matters for the models that project sea level rise and river flow.

Many of them don’t yet represent what happens where a glacier meets a lake, the authors wrote. Yet the glaciers that can respond this way hold more than half of the world’s glacier area.

The classification counts a glacier as lake-ending if any lake touches its front, however small the contact.

Glaciers with only a sliver of lake may behave more like land-ending ones, so the authors said the real gap between the two groups is probably larger than 57 percent.

Flow speeds were available for 84 percent of glaciers and ice-loss rates for 94 percent. Furthermore, the lake map left out Svalbard and Antarctica.

Cause is also unproven: the study shows lake-ending glaciers lose ice faster, not whether the lakes themselves are responsible.

For communities downstream, the open question is water. Mallalieu said the census did not assess water supplies. But in the Himalaya, where large populations rely on meltwater, glacier lakes are expanding fast, he said.

Better models of these glaciers would give those communities more reliable forecasts of their future water.

Untangling the lakes from the glacier shapes is the next task. It means measuring individual lakes, their depth, temperature and how long they persist, glacier by glacier.

Until that is done, the 57 percent is a difference the world can see and not yet explain.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6360. Hot days with weak winds could become a major problem for the power grid

Climate models project that extreme heat and weak winds will coincide more often, straining power grids as cooling demand rises and wind power drops.

A heat wave feels like a problem of too much: too much sun, too much demand for air conditioning.

For a grid that leans on wind turbines, the problem is also too little.

When extreme heat coincides with unusually weak winds, wind farms can generate less electricity just as demand for air conditioning rises.

A new analysis of 27 climate models projects that these spells of extreme heat and weak winds will become two to eight and a half times more frequent over the world’s land by 2100.

How much more depends on how much carbon dioxide is emitted.

The models also project that the longest such spell each year could last roughly two to four times as long.

Lu Shen and colleagues at Peking University in Beijing led the work, with Meng Qu as first author.

The results are model projections, not measurements, and the range reflects both the emissions path and real disagreement among the models.

The team defined a bad day by two thresholds. The wind at 33 feet (10 meters) had to fall into the slowest 5% of warm-season days while the temperature rose into the hottest 5%.

If heat and calm were unrelated, such days would be rare by chance alone. They aren’t unrelated.

Across the middle and high latitudes, hotter days tend to be calmer.

In parts of the northern high latitudes, Southeast Asia and northern Africa, the two coincided five to eight times more often than chance would predict in a NASA weather record.

From 1980 to 2014, the average patch of land saw about 0.6 such days a year. Russia, the southeastern coasts of the United States and China, and parts of the tropics saw 1.5 to 3 days.

Along the storm tracks between 35 and 65 degrees north, the longest spells ran more than five days.

A spell that long means most of a week of weak wind in the middle of a heat wave, in some of the most densely populated regions on Earth.

Europe’s summer of 2022 is the authors’ example. Persistent heat and weak winds coincided with surging electricity demand and rising prices.

The projections come from a NASA dataset that sharpens 27 global climate models to a grid of about 15 miles (25 kilometers).

Each model was scored against its own 1980 to 2014 climate, so the thresholds for “hot” and “calm” shift with the model rather than with the real world.

The models project more days of extreme heat and unusually weak winds by 2100, with the largest increase under the highest-emissions pathway.

Under the lowest pathway, the rise levels off after mid-century.

The tropics change fastest. Between 30 degrees south and 30 degrees north, the frequency rises by 188% under the lowest pathway and by 934% under the highest. The northern mid-latitudes rise by 106% and 689%.

The spells get longer as well as more common. By 2100, the models project that the longest such spell each year could last 84% to 315% longer worldwide, depending on the emissions pathway.

The team split the increase into four causes: hotter average temperatures, slower average winds, bigger swings in both, and a tighter link between heat and calm. Warming alone accounted for most of the rise in every latitude band.

Winds change differently by region. Between 30 and 60 degrees north, average winds slow by up to 0.07 miles per hour (0.03 meters per second) a decade.

The authors tie that stilling to the Arctic warming faster than the tropics, which flattens the temperature difference that drives wind.

In the tropics, winds pick up slightly, which offsets part of the warming effect.

The jet stream matters too. The models shift the northern jet about 1.6 degrees poleward by 2100. North of roughly 50 degrees, that shift strengthens the pairing of hot days with calm ones, and south of it the pairing weakens.

Twenty-seven models disagree, sometimes widely. To shrink the spread, the team checked which models best reproduced the observed trend in these compound events from 1980 to 2014.

Eight reanalysis datasets supplied the observed trend, and the projections were weighted accordingly.

The correction trimmed the projected global increase by 10% to 25% and cut the disagreement among models by 13% to 24%. The models that track history best now carry more weight, and the forecast tightens.

At the regional level it cut disagreement by 10% to 40%, raising projections for South Asia and Eastern Europe and lowering them for Southeast Asia and New Zealand.

The analysis uses daily averages, and the authors note that averaging smooths away the calmest hours, so the study likely undercounts the most extreme lulls.

The models also underestimate how tightly heat and calm are coupled in the northern high latitudes, which is where the events are most pronounced.

The stakes the authors describe are already visible. In the eastern United States, the PJM grid hit a peak load of 162.7 gigawatts during the July 2026 heat wave, close to its summer record.

India set a demand record of 270.73 gigawatts in May 2026, with outages in places. Europe’s June 2026 heat wave was linked to more than 10,000 excess deaths.

The authors flag the hours after sunset. Solar output disappears while demand stays high, and nights are expected to warm faster than days. European minimums already exceed 68°F (20°C) on so-called tropical nights.

The authors’ answer is long-duration storage to carry daytime solar power into those evenings, more mixing of renewable sources, and above all a lower emissions path.

In their projections, the odds of a spell of extreme heat and weak winds by 2100 are four to eight times higher under the higher-emissions pathways than under the lowest one.

What the models can’t yet say is how often the calmest hours, rather than the calmest days, will coincide with the hottest ones.

Answering that would take hourly projections the downscaled dataset doesn’t provide.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

In recent animal tests, tiny robots released into the bloodstream showed promise for treating blood clots.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microrobots controlled by magnets can sweep drugs towards hard-to-reach blood clots in the body, boosting the efficacy of these life-saving treatments, early tests in animals suggest.

In tests with pigs, the microbots helped to dissolve clots around 10 times faster than medication alone. The research team is now working on further safety testing to ready the technology for eventual human trials.

"The whole construct is inspired by nature," said lead researcher Simone Schürle, professor of medical microsystems at ETH Zürich. "There are these tiny bacteria that have little magnetic backbones which they use to navigate with the Earth's magnetic field, and we were really struck by the physics and the properties of them when exposed to rotating magnetic fields," Schürle told Live Science.

ETH Zürich announced the research in a statement on Nov. 9. It has not been described in a peer-reviewed study yet.

Left untreated, blood clots can cause life-threatening damage. These blockages can restrict the flow of blood to the body's key tissues, triggering serious cardiovascular events, such as heart attacks or strokes, which starve cells of oxygen.

Doctors can either remove clots manually with tools or deliver clot-dissolving drugs, called thrombolytics, close to the site of the blockage. However, getting these medications through the final few millimeters of their journey is often the hardest part.

"When a pipe becomes blocked in a branched pipe system, the fluid encounters greater resistance and instead flows through alternative routes where it can pass more easily," Schürle explained. "So when you then try to bring in drugs to dissolve the clot, they won't flow into this area because it's occluded [blocked off]."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This is where microbots can help. The bots are tiny particles whose movements can be controlled by external magnets, which send them rotating and tumbling through blood vessels. These bots can redirect the interrupted blood flow and thus carry essential drugs straight to their target, Schürle and her team say.

Each bullet-shaped microbot contains a magnetic backbone of iron oxide nanoparticles, which is surrounded by a protective sheath of hydrogel polymer. When exposed to a rotating magnetic field, the microbots essentially start to somersault through the blood vessel, creating little vortices that help carry the drugs along with them.

Crucially, the bots' rigid backbone ensures that they spin predictably, while the gel body prevents the particles from sticking together and forming a clump.

The researchers introduce the tiny robots into blood vessels where clots are present.

The robots' motion helps to direct blood-clot-dissolving drugs toward the clots in question.

The team first tested the microbots in a silicon model of a blood vessel that contained clots of pigs' blood. Aided by the rotating microparticles, a thrombolytic drug dissolved the blockages around 10 times faster than medication alone did. That's a potentially life-saving difference, the researchers said.

They then repeated the experiment in live pigs, placing clots in vessels in each of the animals' kidneys. "When we introduced our micro-robots with a conventional, state-of-the-art drug, we could reperfuse [restore blood flow to] a much larger area than if only the drug was there," Schürle said. "The next step is doing safety studies over a longer time and in larger animals."

Earlier safety studies in mice showed that both the iron oxide and the gel sheath polymer safely break down in the body within a few weeks. However, the team will now need to demonstrate that the device is safe in larger mammals before it can be trialed in human patients; their latest test in pigs did not look at how the device broke down or how the pigs fared after the clots were dissolved.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that the bots could be injected into the body alongside the thrombolytic medicine. Once inside, they'd be controlled by targeted electromagnets, making the technique easy to integrate into existing clinical procedures for treating clots.

The team's research is still undergoing peer review, but Schürle has applied for a patent for the microbots' production, which uses a droplet-based microfluidics technique to form each individual particle.

"It's a very cheap, high throughput method to produce the micro-robots," she said. "It's about improving the [clot-dissolving] procedure where it is lacking and helping the drugs travel the last millimeters to be really effective."

Victoria Atkinson is a freelance science journalist, specializing in chemistry and its interface with the natural and human-made worlds. Currently based in York (UK), she formerly worked as a science content developer at the University of Oxford, and later as a member of the Chemistry World editorial team. Since becoming a freelancer, Victoria has expanded her focus to explore topics from across the sciences and has also worked with Chemistry Review, Neon Squid Publishing and the Open University, amongst others. She has a DPhil in organic chemistry from the University of Oxford.

#6358. Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images)

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

#6357. Blood proteins may flag prostate cancer risk more than a decade before diagnosis

Oxford found men's blood differed 15 years before a prostate cancer blood test or diagnosis, with an immune protein among the clearest signs.

The blood test men know for prostate cancer measures one protein, PSA, which is made by the prostate itself. In blood drawn from about 2,500 European men in the 1990s, researchers at Oxford measured more than 6,000 proteins instead.

The men diagnosed with prostate cancer more than 15 years later already differed in a dozen of them.

One of the clearest differences was an immune protein those men had less of, not more. None of the proteins is ready to become a test, the team said. Most of the differences were modest, and not all of them held up in other groups of men.

Zhe Huang, a postdoctoral epidemiologist at Oxford Population Health, part of the University of Oxford, led the work with senior authors Karl Smith-Byrne and Ruth Travis.

“Prostate cancer is not one disease. Many prostate cancers grow slowly and may never cause harm, while others are aggressive and can be life-threatening,” Huang said.

The samples came from EPIC, a European health study that recruited more than half a million people in the 1990s and stored their blood.

Huang’s team picked 982 men from Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and the United Kingdom who later developed prostate cancer. They compared them with a random sample of 1,573 men from the same study, followed for a median of about 16 years.

Men who developed the disease were a median of about six years older when they gave their blood. So the analysis adjusted for age, along with body mass index, smoking, drinking and education.

The idea was to compare the blood itself, not the men’s ages.

A lab platform called SomaScan measured more than 6,400 proteins in each sample. The team asked which proteins differed years ahead of any diagnosis, and separately which differed ahead of an aggressive cancer.

Aggressive meant high grade, spread beyond the prostate, a very high PSA at diagnosis, or death from the disease, and 290 men fit that definition.

The researchers linked twelve proteins to prostate cancer diagnosed more than 15 years after the blood draw. The clearest was GZMK, a protein made by the immune cells that recognize and destroy abnormal cells.

Men with more GZMK in their blood were less likely to be diagnosed, and the longer the gap to diagnosis, the stronger that link became.

The authors offered two readings. More GZMK may mean the immune system is doing a better job of clearing early abnormal cells.

Or the men who later developed cancer may have had fewer of those cells in the blood because the cells had moved into the prostate.

In an interview with Earth.com, Huang and Smith-Byrne said researchers generally consider prostate cancer an immunologically “cold” tumor, one that tends to draw a weak immune response.

“This raises interesting questions about the role of the immune system in the very early stages of cancer development,” they added.

Two proteins tied to inflammation, IL-17B and OSCAR, ran the other way. Higher levels went with higher long-term risk.

Seven proteins were linked to aggressive prostate cancer. Researchers linked one of them, ANKRD1, to every serious form of the disease examined. These included cancers that had spread and cancers that proved fatal, the authors wrote.

Another, AMIGO2, linked to aggressive disease, and most strongly to cancers that had grown beyond the prostate.

This is an adhesion molecule, part of how cells attach to their surroundings, and lab studies have tied it to the process by which tumor cells break away and travel.

FLT4, a receptor involved in growing new blood and lymph vessels, was linked to nearly every outcome the team measured.

The strongest single protein was KLK3, which is PSA under its gene name. Higher PSA levels years earlier increased a man’s likelihood of receiving a diagnosis later.

That isn’t surprising, the authors wrote, because a high PSA reading is what sends a man for a biopsy in the first place.

The team also looked at 71 genes already known to drive prostate cancer when they mutate, and asked whether the proteins those genes produce showed up differently in blood. Five did.

Proteins made by three of those genes, ERBB3, KRAS and NRAS, were linked to aggressive cancers diagnosed about a decade later.

The driver-gene result was the one that surprised the two researchers most.

“These genes are well established in prostate cancer biology, so it was quite surprising to find that their circulating protein products were associated with aggressive prostate cancer,” Huang and Smith-Byrne said.

That doesn’t mean the cancer was already there when the blood was drawn, the authors wrote. Nor is a protein level in blood proof that the gene itself has gone wrong.

Their reading is that the proteins mark early disturbances in the biological pathways to which those genes belong.

The team checked its findings against a U.S. study of 4,284 men, 590 of whom developed prostate cancer. Only about half of the proteins had been measured there.

Two of them, KLK3 and ACP3, another prostate protein, were clearly linked to the disease there too, and two more showed the same direction of association.

Several others, including OSCAR, AMIGO2 and FLT4, were associated in opposite directions in Black and White men. The U.S. study had too few Black participants to settle which direction is real, the authors wrote.

In the U.K. Biobank, 18 of the proteins had been measured with a different technology, and the two platforms agreed poorly.

None of those proteins was linked to prostate cancer there. Genetic analyses supported a handful, including AMIGO2, KLK3 and OSCAR.

The aggressive-cancer results also come from fewer men. Tumor grade was unknown for 31 percent of the cases and stage for 46 percent, and only 102 men died of the disease.

Some of the associations may be chance, the authors wrote, and the study had no information on family history.

Whether any of these blood proteins can predict a man’s prostate cancer risk better than his age and PSA already do hasn’t been tested.

The findings still have to be confirmed in larger and more diverse groups of men, Huang and Smith-Byrne said. Their study also mainly looked for proteins that may help a prostate cancer develop, not proteins that could spot a cancer already there.

“Developing a blood test for early detection would require further dedicated prediction studies,” they told Earth.com.

Huang said measuring thousands of proteins in blood collected years early lets researchers begin to ask how men who later develop aggressive prostate cancer differ from men who don’t.

The next step runs through a Cancer Research U.K. program on prostate cancer causes and prevention, which the team said will test whether the findings can improve prediction or prevention.

Some of the proteins may even play a causal role in how the cancer develops, the two researchers said.

“If confirmed by future experimental and clinical studies, this could open up exciting opportunities for earlier prevention, potentially even through approaches such as cancer vaccines,” they said.

For now, the GZMK result is a clue rather than a tool. Men who were never diagnosed had more of an immune protein in their blood 15 years earlier. Whether measuring it would help any patient is the question still open.

The full study was published in the journal European Urology.

#6356. The Sky Today on Monday, November 23: Double star Kurhah in Cepheus

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 22: Flat-floored lunar crater Schickard

A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

If you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST on November 24, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon. A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars.

This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so big and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

#6355. Scientists can now uncover a person’s age, sex, diet, and DNA all from just one single tooth

Forensic scientists sliced a single tooth from each of 15 unidentified bodies and read birth year, age, sex, DNA, diet, and drug use from it.

By the time a body is discovered months or years after death, the face, fingerprints, and clothing are usually long gone. The remaining bones can give investigators a rough idea of sex and age, but that age estimate can be wrong by up to 30 years. Turns out, a single tooth holds far more answers.

A team in Japan took a single tooth from each of 15 such bodies. From that tooth alone, they worked out each person’s birth year, age at death, sex, and DNA profile.

The same tooth also showed what kind of diet the person grew up on and which drugs they had been taking.

Hisako Saitoh, an associate professor of forensic dentistry at the Institute of Science Tokyo, led the work with her doctoral student, Sayaka Yamada.

Fuyuki Tokanai of the Center for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry at Yamagata University was also on the team. Colleagues at the University of Tokyo and Chiba University took part as well.

All 15 people were unidentified when they reached the autopsy table. Five were skeletal remains, ten were badly decomposed. Fourteen of them were later identified.

“Different tissues within a tooth preserve different forensic information. By combining multiple analytical methods, we sought to obtain as many clues as possible from a single tooth,” Saitoh said.

Bone is full of tiny channels for blood vessels and marrow. This means that soil, moisture, and microbes can get into it after death. Enamel is the hardest material in the human body, and it seals the crown of a tooth.

A thin layer called cementum wraps around the root, and this keeps outside substances away from the soft pulp inside.

A tooth also stops changing once it has formed. Bone rebuilds itself throughout life, but enamel laid down in early childhood stays chemically the same until death.

That makes a tooth a sealed record of the years when it grew. This explains why researchers have used teeth to track where a mammoth or an elephant once lived.

Earlier forensic teams had combined several of these tests, but they used several teeth per person, or a tooth plus a toenail, and the bodies hadn’t been dead for long.

Saitoh’s team wanted to know how much information one tooth could provide after a body had been lying outdoors for months or years.

The team chose the lower first premolar, the tooth just behind the canine. Its crown finishes forming at about age five, so its enamel records the first years of life. It has a single root, it’s easy to pull, and the lips cover the gap it leaves.

Each tooth was washed, dried overnight, and cut lengthwise into slices about 1/25 of an inch (1 millimeter) thick, which is thinner than a dime.

Enamel from one slice went to a radiocarbon lab, and a root slice rich in cementum went to DNA testing. Dentin from the other side went to an age test, and the central slice holding the pulp went to drug screening.

The age test relies on a slow chemical change. Amino acids in living tissue come in a left-handed form, and over a lifetime a small share flips to the right-handed mirror image.

The team measured that share in the dentin and read the person’s age off a curve built from six other premolars of known age.

The birth year came from radiocarbon, but not the kind used on fossils. Nuclear weapons tests in the 1950s and early 1960s sharply raised the amount of radioactive carbon in the air. The level peaked in 1963 and has been falling ever since.

Enamel forming in a child’s mouth took up whatever level was in the air at the time, so its carbon shows when it formed. Scientists have used the same spike to age a whale from its teeth.

The catch is that the curve rises and then falls, so one reading usually matches two possible years. For one man, the enamel gave a birth year of either 1955 or 1979.

Adding the age-at-death estimate settled it. A birth in 1979 plus his estimated 58 years would put his death in 2036, so he was born in 1955. His real birth year was 1957.

Across the 15 people, the radiocarbon ranges included the true birth year in 14 cases. The age-at-death estimates on their own were off by about eight years on average.

Once the two tests were combined, the birth-year estimates landed within about five years of the truth, on average.

DNA from the cementum slice gave the person’s sex in all 15 cases. In 12 of them it also produced a profile with enough genetic markers to match against a relative or a database.

The same kind of DNA work has recently corrected the story of a Roman-era skeleton in England and been read from Neanderthal teeth.

The pulp slice went through a drug screen covering 251 substances, and every one of the 15 teeth contained something, even if only caffeine. In nine cases the drugs in the tooth matched at least some of what the original autopsy had found in blood or muscle.

In five cases they matched prescriptions the person was known to have been taking, including antidepressants and antipsychotics.

The tooth didn’t catch everything, however. Drugs that appeared to have been taken shortly before death showed up in stomach contents and muscle at autopsy but not in the tooth.

Saitoh’s team suggested that drugs move into a tooth slowly, so a tooth reflects long-term use rather than a last dose.

The fifteenth body belonged to a man who has never been definitively identified. His tooth put his birth year at either 1956 or 1976, and his dentin put his age at about 38.

The 1956 option would mean he died in 1995, long before his body was found in 2013, so the team’s answer is a man born in 1976.

Investigators currently believe he was born around 1972 and was about 41 when he died. The two readings disagree by four years, which is inside the method’s average error of about five years.

The tooth gives investigators a second, independent estimate of who he might be.

Stable carbon in the enamel added a rough picture of childhood diet. All 15 readings fit a diet built on rice and wheat rather than corn, which is consistent with a traditional Japanese diet.

The authors wrote that carbon alone can’t say where someone grew up.

The errors here were larger than in earlier studies that ran each test on its own. The birth-year estimates were least accurate for people born before the fallout spike began to climb and for those born in more recent years, when the curve had flattened.

The age test usually works best on dentin from the center of the tooth. Here the center was needed for the drug screen. Instead, the team used dentin from the outer part, and that may have cost some accuracy.

One tooth also produced radiocarbon dates between the 600s and 800s AD, centuries before the woman could have been born.

That sample had the highest carbon content of the set, and the authors suspect carbon from outside the body had got into the enamel.

The team’s next step is more cases, and a closer look at exactly where in a tooth each slice should come from.

“Moving forward, we aim to further improve the accuracy and reproducibility of each biochemical analytical method demonstrated in this study and establish standardized methods that can be widely applied in routine forensic medical and dental practice,” Saitoh said.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.
