Up to 15 shooting stars per hour may be visible as the Leonids peak under dark skies tonight (Nov. 16 - 17), with the moon setting before the best viewing hours.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of November's best meteor showers peaks tonight (Nov. 16-17) and is expected to bring up to 15 "shooting stars" per hour to a near-moonless night sky.

Although the annual Leonid meteor shower, which is famous for occasionally producing spectacular meteor storms, is active from Nov. 6 to Nov. 30, the peak on Monday into Tuesday is the best time to look, according to the American Meteor Society.

Although the Leonids typically produce around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions, they're among the year's fastest shooting stars, reaching 43 miles per second (70 kilometers per second), and often produce bright meteors that leave glowing trails.

The best time to see them is between midnight and dawn Tuesday (Nov. 17), when the constellation Leo, from which the meteors appear to radiate, climbs higher in the eastern sky. However, shooting stars can appear anywhere in the sky.

A 45%-lit waxing crescent moon will set just before midnight, leaving dark skies for meteor watching. For the best views, find a spot away from artificial lights, lie back with a wide view of the sky, and allow about 20 minutes for your eyes to become adapted to the dark. Don't use binoculars or a telescope during a meteor shower; they will only restrict your view. However, you can try your hand at photographing the shower with your smartphone or a good astrophotography camera.

The Leonids are produced by tiny particles of dust and debris left behind in the inner solar system by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which takes about 33 years to orbit the sun and is about 2.2 miles (3.6 km) in diameter. Tempel-Tuttle last visited the inner solar system in 1998 and is due to return again in 2031.

Although no rapid-fire "meteor storms" are expected this year, the Leonids are famous for occasionally producing outbursts of 1,000 shooting stars per hour. Such storms occurred in 1833, 1866, 1966, 1999, 2001 and 2002, according to the American Meteor Society. The next storm is expected to hit in 2099.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

After the Leonids, the next major meteor shower will be the Geminids, which peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. The Geminid meteor shower, which is caused by an asteroid rather than a comet, can produce up to 120 meteors per hour. This year, the Geminids will peak in dark skies, thanks to a slim crescent moon setting shortly after dark on Dec. 13.

Jamie Carter is a Cardiff, U.K.-based freelance science journalist and a regular contributor to Live Science. He is the author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners and co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and leads international stargazing and eclipse-chasing tours. His work appears regularly in Space.com, Forbes, New Scientist, BBC Sky at Night, Sky & Telescope, and other major science and astronomy publications. He is also the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com.

#6353. Ice Age humans were far less isolated than scientists assumed, according to a 30,000-year-old woman’s DNA

Ice Age Europeans mixed across the continent earlier than genetics had shown, according to a 30,000-year-old genome and DNA from cave dirt.

Most people imagine Ice Age Europe as a patchwork of tiny hunting bands living out their lives in isolated valleys, far from any other group.

Archaeologists have doubted that version of history for a long time. This is mainly due to the fact that the same styles of tools and carvings show up across the entire continent. Even so, DNA from Ice Age samples has mostly supported the isolated view.

A woman who died around 30,000 years ago in what is now southwestern France has changed that.

Most of her ancestry came from the western European people of her time. However, part of it also came from populations related to central and eastern Europe. The mixing happened roughly 32,500 to 31,500 years ago.

The analysis of her DNA now gives the oldest set of genome-wide data from a modern human in southwestern Europe.

Pere Gelabert and Ron Pinhasi of the University of Vienna‘s Department of Evolutionary Anthropology led the work. Their co-authors include researchers at Harvard Medical School, the University of Cantabria and the University of New Mexico.

The study rests on DNA from three new Ice Age individuals and one sample of cave sediment. Thus, the picture it draws is built from very few people.

The bone fragment of the woman was recovered from Isturitz Cave in the Basque Country, western Pyrenees. Excavators dug it up in the 1950s, and it stayed in a Paris institute for over 60 years. Then, in 2013, Pinhasi took a sample from it for DNA analysis.

The team recovered more than 454,000 of the genetic markers it was looking for. This represents one of the richest Gravettian datasets yet.

Gravettian is the name for the culture that spread across Europe during the onset of the last Ice Age, between about 34,000 and 25,000 years ago. This culture is known for its shared tool styles, burial practices and portable art.

Until now, DNA data from this Ice Age period in Europe sorted into two stable groups, a western one and a central-eastern one, with little sign of contact between them.

The Isturitz woman belongs mostly to the western group. But several tests also found a share of her ancestry related to the ancestors of people buried at Dolní Věstonice in what is now the Czech Republic.

In an interview with Earth.com, Gelabert said the find overturned a long-held assumption.

“Until this new genomic data, we assumed that the people in Southwestern Europe were quite the same for more than 20,000 years,” he said.

The new data, he said, point to population movements that were probably continental in scale, and that the team doesn’t yet clearly understand.

Isturitz is one of the richest Ice Age sites in southern Europe, with an unusual number of carved objects and signs of repeated, intensive occupation.

Archaeologists have long argued that it was a gathering place where different groups met to hunt, trade, socialize and find partners. The cave lies at the natural passage between the rest of Europe and the Iberian Peninsula.

The woman isn’t alone. When the team reanalyzed a previously published genome from Ormesson, near Paris, dated to about 31,800 to 30,000 years ago, it found a similar eastern signal.

In addition, Belgian individuals from Goyet Cave, about 28,000 to 26,000 years old, were already known to carry mixed ancestry.

Two explanations are possible, the authors wrote. People from the east may have moved west during the Gravettian itself. Or the eastern-looking ancestry may be an older component, already in western Europe before 35,000 years ago.

The team favors the first. The DNA signal is absent from earlier Ice Age genomes in the same region, and it vanishes from southwestern Europe after 30,000 years ago.

At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, northern Spain, the team took two pinches of sediment, 0.002 ounces (50 milligrams) each.

They came from a layer dated to about 22,100 to 21,700 years ago, the coldest stretch of the last Ice Age, when human remains are extremely rare. No bone or tooth was needed, only the dirt that people had walked on.

The researchers built nine DNA libraries from those two extracts and sequenced them 101 times. Out of roughly a billion DNA fragments, more than 294,000 were human.

After the team kept only fragments showing the chemical damage of real ancient DNA, 14,737 genetic markers remained, enough to read the ancestry of the people who used the cave.

The sediment’s ancestry matched the western group, the Isturitz woman’s lineage, so that ancestry persisted in the region through the coldest millennia.

“Sedimentary DNA allows us to recover genetic information from periods where human remains are missing,” Pinhasi said. “This gives us a way to connect archaeological layers with the genetic ancestry of the people who occupied a site.”

Gelabert told Earth.com the team had recovered DNA from this cave’s sediment before. “What surprised us this time is that the quality is unmatched,” he said.

He described the sample as one of the richest sources of human DNA ever reported. For the first time in the region’s Upper Paleolithic, he said, it let the team tie a culture to a group of people.

The third new genome came from Ostuni Cave in southern Italy and belongs to a male fetus about 27,800 to 27,400 years old.

The team identified him as a first-degree relative of a woman from the same cave whose genome was already published. He was most likely her son.

Comparing the two showed that his father came from the same population as his mother, as far as the data can tell. Yet the parents were not close relatives.

The boy’s genome carried no long stretches of identical DNA from both parents, and the population he came from was genetically larger than any other Gravettian group measured so far.

Gelabert said this is the first mother-and-fetus pair of genomes from the European Paleolithic, and that comparing them is what showed how genetically diverse her population was.

All three individuals, and the people in the El Mirón sediment, are predicted to have had dark skin, dark hair and brown eyes. That was the usual pattern for Europeans of that era.

The whole Gravettian, Solutrean and Epigravettian record, three Ice Age cultures, rests on genome-wide data from fewer than 50 people. This study adds an extra three.

The third is a tooth from Chufín Cave in Cantabria, dated to about 26,000 years ago. It was so degraded that it yielded fewer than 20,000 markers, enough to place it in the western group and little more.

Sediment has its own limits. The DNA in it comes from several people mixed together, and the team’s reading suggests more of them were male than female. The date for the east-west mixing also assumes it happened in a single pulse.

The study does not settle where the eastern ancestry came from. The authors wrote that no particular central European group stands out as the source, and that no genome from the earlier Aurignacian culture exists for southwestern Europe to compare against.

The team did find one thing the data argue against. Earlier work on tooth shapes had suggested a population turnover in western Europe around 28,000 years ago.

The new genomes, the sediment and the reanalyzed published data instead show the same western ancestry in place from 30,000 to 20,000 years ago.

Asked by Earth.com what comes next, Gelabert returned to the sediment.

“Next step is clearly to find out when the population movements that we see in Isturitz really happened. Sediment will be key for this goal,” he said.

The authors named a target: the Aurignacian layers of Isturitz itself, deposits older than the woman, which could show whether the eastern signal was already there before she was born.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6352. Air pollution may weaken one of the brain’s natural defenses against dementia

A mouse study suggests that fine particles in polluted air can weaken the brain’s protective barrier, offering a clue to the link between air pollution and dementia.

Air pollution has been linked to dementia for years. It is difficult, however, to work out what happens inside the brain between the time a person breathes in polluted air and the onset of memory problems.

An experiment in Ohio has provided some clues. After months of breathing polluted air, laboratory mice kept their weight, groomed themselves and went about their usual activities without obvious signs of distress.

Put those same mice in a maze they had already learned to navigate, though, and something was wrong.

Changes had taken place inside their brains, even in animals that had no genetic predisposition to Alzheimer’s-like disease.

Before working with mice, the team examined health records from 475,325 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2010.

The median age at enrollment was 58. Over a median follow-up period of nearly 14 years, 12,758 participants developed Alzheimer’s disease or a related dementia or died of an Alzheimer’s-related cause.

The researchers wanted to know how much of the risk was associated with where people lived and how much was associated with their genes.

Higher levels of fine particle pollution were linked to dementia, even after accounting for factors such as smoking and diabetes.

People with greater inherited susceptibility also faced higher risk, although the combined association was smaller than expected if the two individual effects multiplied.

For the animal experiments, the team used air collected outdoors in Cleveland, Ohio.

The particles of interest were PM2.5, a group of airborne particles measuring about one ten-thousandth of an inch (2.5 micrometers) or less.

The samples contained a mixture of substances associated with dust and combustion, including iron, nickel and copper.

The team concentrated the particles until their levels reached roughly 10 times those measured outdoors in Cleveland. The resulting concentration was comparable to the average reported for New Delhi in 2023.

At just four weeks old, mice began breathing either this polluted air or filtered air for eight hours a day, five days a week. Among them were animals carrying five genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s disease.

Sixteen weeks into the experiment, the team began testing the animals’ memory.

One test involved a circular platform with an escape hole. Over three days, the mice had repeated opportunities to learn where the hole was, followed by a two-day break before their final test.

Ordinary mice breathing polluted air had about as much difficulty finding the hole as Alzheimer’s-prone mice breathing filtered air. The genetically vulnerable mice exposed to pollution struggled the most.

Other tests revealed problems recognizing unfamiliar objects, weaker muscles in the front and back legs, and behavior consistent with increased anxiety.

Blood vessels in the brain have a protective barrier that limits what can pass from the blood into surrounding brain tissue. Without a properly functioning barrier, potentially harmful substances have easier access to that tissue.

To check for leaks, the team used three chemical markers, including a blue dye.

Much more of these substances escaped from blood vessels in pollution-exposed mice than in ordinary mice breathing filtered air.

Some of the leakage measurements, however, came from groups of as few as two animals.

The brains of exposed mice also contained higher levels of several chemicals involved in inflammation.

Whether the inflammation damaged blood vessels or whether other processes contributed to both problems remains unclear.

Within the hippocampus, a region involved in forming memories, lies a smaller area called the dentate gyrus. New brain cells continue to form there after birth in mice.

Interestingly, pollution did not significantly affect how many new cells ordinary mice produced. The problem was keeping those cells alive, as fewer survived over a period of 30 days.

In mice prone to Alzheimer’s disease, both the production and survival of new cells suffered.

Pollution also disturbed the balance between two forms of a molecule called NAD, which cells depend on for energy production and processes involved in repairing damage.

Much of the investigation centered on microglia, the immune cells that live inside the brain. Sanjay Rajagopalan, a professor of medicine at Case Western Reserve University, co-led the work.

“By recreating in mice what happens when people breath polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain’s immune cells,” said Sanjay Rajagopalan.

When the researchers compared polluted-air and filtered-air groups, they identified changes in the activity of 766 genes in ordinary mice. They also found that genetic background influenced how 2,876 genes responded to pollution.

“These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world’s population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it,” Rajagopalan said.

Alzheimer’s disease is associated with the accumulation of a protein called amyloid in the brain. As the protein collects, it forms deposits known as plaques.

Despite examining brain tissue with two different staining methods, the team could not find these plaques in ordinary mice that had breathed polluted air. Their memory problems had developed without detectable amyloid buildup.

Andrew Pieper, a professor of translational psychiatry at Case Western Reserve University, was also a senior author.

“We’ve identified a key way that air pollution harms the healthy brain and speeds up Alzheimer’s disease,” said Andrew Pieper.

How much pollution each person actually breathed remains unknown. The team estimated exposure using home addresses.

Only white participants and male mice were studied. Gene analysis involved just three mice per group.

“This helps us understand how factors in our environment can accelerate and intensify brain diseases of aging. It also opens the door to studying other environmental stresses on the brain, and to finding ways to keep the brain resilient even when we can’t avoid those stressors,” Pieper said.

Air pollution’s role in human dementia needs further investigation. But unlike inherited risk, pollution can be reduced.

The full study was published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation.

#6351. Rainbow trout faced a familiar virus, but tiny plastic fibers changed their chances of survival

In a lab study, young rainbow trout exposed to nylon microfibers were less likely to survive a common fish virus.

Microplastics come in many shapes, and a new study on rainbow trout suggests the shape matters.

In an eight-week experiment, young trout exposed to both nylon microplastic fibers and a common fish virus had roughly double the odds of dying compared with trout exposed to the virus alone.

Trout that lived with round nylon particles of similar width fared no worse than fish with no plastic at all.

The fibers didn’t kill fish on their own. Without the virus, plastic of either shape made no difference to survival.

The study came from the Virginia Institute of Marine Science at William & Mary, where Meredith Evans Seeley, Robert Hale and Andrew Wargo work. Anna Mehlhorn, an undergraduate at the time, is now at Cornell.

“Not all plastics are created equal, and so that creates an opportunity to identify the worst forms of pollution and come up with solutions,” Wargo said.

Three years ago, the same group reported that microplastics made a trout virus deadlier. Nylon microfibers stood out: in that earlier work, fish exposed to them faced a hazard of death 6.4 times that of fish given the virus alone.

“We saw the effect with the nylon fibers and had to ask, ‘Is it the fact it’s a fiber or is it the fact that it was nylon?'” Hale said.

To answer that, the team kept the material the same and changed the shape. The fibers were about 0.02 inches (500 micrometers) long and 10 micrometers wide, the kind that shed from synthetic fabric.

The powder was made of rounded nylon grains averaging 15 to 20 micrometers across, about as wide as the fibers but nowhere near as long.

The team raised 800 juvenile rainbow trout in 40 tanks of 20 fish each. Every other day, the plastic groups got a dose of fibers or powder in their water, and the tank sat still for a day before it was flushed.

Most groups got plastic for the full eight weeks; two fiber groups got it only in the first or last four.

Halfway through, half the tanks were dosed with infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus, a major cause of losses on trout farms.

Fish started dying a few days later, and the dying largely ended within about two weeks.

By the end, 39% of the trout exposed to both the virus and eight weeks of fibers were alive. In tanks that got the virus with no plastic, 56% survived, and in tanks with neither, 86% did.

In the statistical model, eight weeks of fibers raised the odds of death 2.03 times compared with no particles.

None of the other plastic treatments had a significant effect, including the round powder for eight weeks and the fibers given only before or only after the virus.

The team also sampled tank water every few days to measure how much virus the fish were shedding. Shedding peaked three days after the virus went in and fell to undetectable levels by day 47 in every treatment.

The plastic groups did not differ, though the eight-week fiber tanks showed a trend toward the highest peaks.

The authors wrote that measuring shedding from groups of fish in only four tanks per treatment may have limited the study’s power. A few super-shedders could mask the rest.

So the fibers did not seem to make the virus more abundant. They seemed to make the fish easier to infect.

The researchers suspect the long, stiff fibers damage protective tissue such as the gills, which they described in the university’s account as the fibers’ pokiness.

“It’s likely creating an easier path for that virus to infect that host,” Seeley said.

If microplastic fibers open a door for the virus, the damage has to be there before the virus arrives, and it probably has to keep up afterward. That is what the tanks showed.

Fibers given only after infection did about as well as no plastic. Fibers given only before the virus pushed mortality up toward the chronic group’s level, but the difference was not significant.

The authors pointed to tissue damage from plastic in other animals. In seabirds, scarring from swallowed plastic has been given its own name, plasticosis. Inflammation from microplastics is also under study in fish and in human tissue.

“One of the things that was becoming clear to us is that microplastics have really significant impacts, but they’re not always lethal,” Seeley said.

The team used one high concentration of plastic, 10 milligrams per liter, to make the effect easy to see. The authors wrote that future work should test a range of doses to find the levels that matter in real water.

The fibers and the powder were also not chemically identical, since the fibers were a stiffer grade of nylon.

The work was funded by the NOAA Marine Debris Program. The group is now working with a commercial trout farm to find out which microplastics turn up in working tanks and where they come from.

Trout farms use nylon line and other plastic gear that can break down into microplastics, and the particles are also common in the water where wild fish live.

Earlier work has shown that microplastics can carry microbes and change how pathogens behave.

People are also exposed to microplastic fibers through indoor dust. The authors wrote that the results call for research into whether microplastics change the course of infectious disease in wildlife and people.

They also want to know which features of a particle, such as rigidity and length, do the damage.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry.

#6350. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”

#6349. Nov. 23, 1221: The birth of Alfonso the Wise

On Nov. 23, 1221, Alfonso X was born in Spain, the son of King Ferdinand III of Castile and Leon. By the time he succeeded his father in 1252, Alfonso was already known as a scholar – though he demonstrated his military might as well, putting down several revolts and annexing Murcia.

Known as Alfonso the Wise, the king pioneered efforts to translate Arabic and Andalusian works of astronomy into the vernacular Castilian. His multicultural court authored scholarly works and engineered scientific instruments, as well as collecting an extensive library of works on astrology and astronomy. Alfonso also commissioned the Alfosine Tables, astronomical tables based on Arabic sources and updated with new observations – facilitated by new astronomical instruments constructed at Alfonso’s orders. The work included stellar and planetary positions and became the standard for astronomy in Europe for the late medieval and early Renaissance periods.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

A recent satellite photo captured an underwater cloud of fish sperm, or milt, appearing to glow green during a Pacific herring spawning event at a reproductive "sweet spot" along the coast of Canada's Vancouver Island.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Where is it? Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada [48.95586624, -125.42994277]

What's in the photo? A green cloud of milt (fish sperm) and eggs during a Pacific herring spawning event

Which satellite took the photo? Landsat 9

This surprising satellite snap shows a giant underwater plume of fish sperm that seems to glow green beneath the waves. The colorful cloud appeared during a spawning event at a reproductive "sweet spot" along Canada's western coastline.

The striking sight was spotted in Barkley Sound, along a section of the southern coast of Vancouver Island in British Columbia, roughly 45 miles (70 kilometers) north of the U.S. border. The bright-green cloud is the most concentrated between Salmon Beach — the triangular town in the center of the image — and the smaller Forbes Island, which is also "glowing" along its northern coast.

The green cloud is around 4 miles (7 km) from end to end and is made of milt — a fluid containing sperm made by fish, mollusks and other aquatic animals — that was released during a Pacific herring (Clupea pallasii) spawning event. Like many other fish species, Pacific herring reproduce by congregating in large groups. The females lay eggs, which stick to kelp, sea grasses and rocky surfaces, before the males release their milt, which disperses over the area and fertilizes the eggs.

Pacific herring, which grow to around 10 inches (25 centimeters) long, often congregate in this spot off Vancouver Island in late winter or early spring, gathering for several weeks before releasing their gametes, or sex cells, according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

"The herring spawn is a really fabulous time to be out here," local resident Ryan Cutler, who used a drone to capture close-up photos of this year's spawning event (see below), told CBC News. "It's a really, really spectacular time to be around."

The cloud of milt arguably looks even more imposing up close, as you can see in this drone photo from resident Ryan Cutler, who described the spawning event as "fabulous" and "spectacular."

Spawning events can last anywhere between a few hours and several days, and scientists are increasingly turning to satellite images to help monitor these occurrences, according to the Earth Observatory. In this case, the milt cloud was visible for around 48 hours.

While the milky substance appears a striking green in these images, it is actually white. It appears green only because it is closer to the surface than the surrounding seafloor, meaning that less reflected light is absorbed by the water. This is also why shallow patches of water often appear turquoise when viewed from above.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The coastline alongside Salmon Beach is perfect for herring to spawn because it strikes the perfect balance between a number of important factors. "Herrings prefer spawning locations that are more protected, have rocky substrate, and allow them to select areas with reduced salinity," Jessica Moffatt, a biologist with Vancouver Island's Island Marine Aquatic Working Group, told the Earth Observatory. "Barkley Sound hits the 'sweet spot' in many of these regards."

The Pacific herring is an important species in this region; it is a primary food source for Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), which give Salmon Beach its name. The herring are also hunted by local First Nation groups, according to CBC News.

During the spawning events, a wide range of other predatory marine life — including large fish, whales and sea lions — are drawn to the area to feast on the herring, according to the Earth Observatory. And on land, eagles, wolves and bears are more likely to appear during the mass reproduction event.

The milt appears green from above due to how wavelengths are absorbed by water as light reflects off the the white substance.

Coincidentally, this exact patch of ocean was the site of one of the weirdest oceanographic events ever seen. In 2020, around 4 miles (7 km) off the coast of Ucluelet (located just along the coastline to the left in the photo), scientists detected a rogue wave that appeared in the open ocean seemingly from nowhere. The massive wave reached the height of a four-story building, making it the most extreme version of this phenomenon ever seen.

Farther offshore, around 150 miles (240 km) south of Vancouver Island, researchers also detected a surprise swarm of more than 2,000 underwater earthquakes in a single day in March 2024, hinting that a section of the seafloor was ripping apart.

A recent satellite photo captured a series of clouds sculpted by von Kármán vortices from a volcano on South Korea's Jeju Island. A giant multicolor plume, ejected by China's Yangtze River, is also visible in the image.

A recent satellite photo captured a gleaming halo of phytoplankton encircling the remote Chatham Islands. The stunning sight is the result of a hidden underwater structure, which has also helped kill hundreds of cetaceans.

A recent satellite photo captured a stunning scene of sediment swirling across the West Florida Shelf after an extreme cold snap that covered large parts of the eastern U.S. in snow.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6346. Prohibition helped save diamondback terrapins from the soup pot, and now a tiny parasite hints their subspecies line may be in the wrong place

A fluke that lives in mudsnails and diamondback terrapins shows a genetic break near the Carolinas border, up to about 186 miles south of the turtles' subspecies line.

Diamondback terrapins are hard to count. They live in scattered coastal marshes, travel little, and are scarce in many places.

A tiny flatworm that depends on them is easier to find. It leaves pearly cysts on mudsnails, and even community volunteers can spot them.

Scientists have now read the DNA of that parasite at marshes from Cape Cod to northeast Florida.

Its populations split near the North Carolina and South Carolina border, up to about 186 miles (300 kilometers) south of where the line between two terrapin subspecies is usually drawn.

The parasite is a fluke called Pleurogonius malaclemys. Adult flukes live and mate in the intestines of diamondback terrapins, and their eggs leave the turtle in its droppings.

Eastern mudsnails then eat the eggs. Inside a snail, the fluke multiplies without mating and sends out larvae that settle on snails, mostly on the plate that seals the shell, as small, pearly cysts.

When a terrapin eats a snail carrying cysts, the cycle starts again.

Because the fluke cannot complete its life without terrapins, its cysts on snails are a sign that terrapins live nearby.

Snails only pick up the fluke as adults, after their drifting larval stage, so the parasite’s travel between marshes is likely to depend mostly on the turtles.

Diamondback terrapins are the only turtle in North America that lives only in brackish coastal water. Until the early 20th century they were hunted heavily for turtle soup, and populations crashed.

Prohibition helped them. In 1920 it banned sherry, a key ingredient in most turtle soup recipes, and the hunting pressure largely faded.

Numbers kept falling anyway, because of habitat loss and terrapins getting caught in crab pots. The coastal marshes they depend on are under threat too, and nearly all of the world’s salt marshes may be underwater by 2100. The species is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List.

The team, led by Garrett Maggio, a Ph.D. candidate at East Carolina University, collected mudsnails at 29 locations between April and October in 2022, 2023 and 2024.

They found the fluke at 23 of them, including new spots on Cape Cod and in Florida that push its known range farther north and south.

Out of 4,293 snails picked haphazardly and dissected, only six carried the fluke inside their bodies. But 553 had cysts. At one marsh in St. Augustine, Florida, cysts showed up on about 74 percent of the snails.

The researchers also examined 38 terrapins from southern New Jersey, all females killed by cars, through a partnership with The Wetlands Institute in Stone Harbor. Seventeen of them, about 45 percent, carried adult flukes, between one and seven per turtle.

Some cysts turned out to be pink instead of pearly. They were first spotted in North Carolina in 2023 and later in Massachusetts and New Jersey. The cause of the color is still unknown.

The scientists sequenced a section of mitochondrial DNA from 476 fluke samples and found 102 different variants. Most of them, 79, turned up at only one location.

Marshes farther apart had more different flukes. One variant was common across most northern marshes, and another was common across most southern ones.

The sharpest change came between Wilmington, North Carolina, and Charleston, South Carolina.

Grouping the marshes at that border explained about three times more of the genetic variation than grouping them at Cape Hatteras, the usual line between the northern diamondback terrapin and the Carolina terrapin.

The authors call the gap noteworthy. Adult female terrapins, the most mobile group, have been found to travel no more than about 5.3 miles (8.5 kilometers). Since the fluke only mates inside terrapins, the result raises questions about where the two subspecies really meet.

“Our findings show that this parasite may provide an important window into the ecology of diamondback terrapins,” said Michael McCoy, senior author and a research professor at FAU Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.

The terrapin subspecies were first described from their body shape, before genetic tools were common.

Studies of terrapin DNA since then have given conflicting answers about how far the turtles move, and one study found gene flow most likely driven by people moving terrapins in the past.

The authors stress that the fluke results are a starting point. They used a single genetic marker that is passed down only through the mother. A direct comparison between fluke DNA and terrapin DNA is still needed to prove the parasite truly mirrors its host.

“Rather than relying exclusively on direct observations of terrapins, we can investigate the organisms that depend on them,” McCoy said.

Parasites make up nearly half of known biodiversity, yet they are rarely included in conservation plans. When a host declines, its parasites can vanish with it, as happened to most of the parasites once carried by New Zealand’s kākāpō.

The authors argue that the terrapin fluke deserves protection alongside its host. They add that the fluke’s wide range is evidence that terrapins are still present along much of the Atlantic coast, despite the threats they face.

The information was obtained from the study published in Ecology and Evolution and from Florida Atlantic University.

#6345. The amazing Crab Nebula

One of my personal favorite objects in the night sky is the Crab Nebula (M1). It’s No. 1 on Charles Messier’s list, although I don’t think he ordered his objects by how cool they are (a missed opportunity!). It’s not exactly impressive visually in most scopes — mostly a gray blob, or a spiky gray blob in larger apertures — but it’s one of those targets that if you know what you are looking at, it becomes immensely more interesting to observe.

The Crab Nebula burst onto the scene in 1054 C.E., when a massive star in the constellation Taurus collapsed in on itself in a supernova whose light was visible during the day, as documented by multiple civilizations around the world. Its leftover shell of gas and dust has been expanding ever since, and the bright glow is still visible thanks to what remains of the progenitor star: a rapidly spinning neutron star, known as a pulsar. The “crab” moniker stems from a drawing made by the William Parsons, Earl of Rosse, in the early 1840s with a 36-inch telescope, which depicts crab-leg-like appendages, although he later noted that observations through a 72-inch resulted in a view that looked rather different than his original drawing.

Pulsars are some of the most extreme objects in the universe. The Crab Pulsar, which is approximately 12–17 miles (20–28 kilometers) in diameter, spins at a breakneck 30 times per second — once every 33 milliseconds. At magnitude 16.6, it is a very difficult catch, but possible in large (20-plus-inch) scopes on nights with steady skies. It sits only a few arcseconds from a slightly brighter magnitude 15.8 star that guides the way. The pulsar produces a relativistic-speed stellar wind that generates synchrotron radiation, which occurs when charged particles move along curved paths, bent by strong magnetic fields. This is seen across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, from radio to gamma rays, forming the main diffuse part of the nebula’s emission. This radiation has a total luminosity some 100,000 times greater than the Sun’s! The pulsar is slowing down gradually as a result of energy carried away by its stellar wind, increasing its period by 36 nanoseconds per day.

The nebula is still expanding, even nearly 1,000 years later, at a rate of 3.4 million mph (5.5 million km/h) — that’s 950 miles (1,527 km) per second, or 0.5% the speed of light! While not noticeable in a single observation, comparing images across several years shows the expansion on very human-accessible timescales.

The Crab’s intricate filaments are what make it so visually stunning in images. These structures are the remnants of the star’s atmosphere, consisting of gases like ionized helium, hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, iron, neon, and sulfur. It’s a moderately tricky astrophotography target to process: In wideband, it has a largely gray interior wrapped in red tendrils, so it is best imaged in narrowband, where it can display incredible, intricate detail that looks well and truly alien. A famous colorful 2005 Hubble image uses narrowband light from oxygen and sulfur and has oxygen-III set as red, sulfur-II as green, and oxygen-I as blue. When I’ve shot the Crab, I used hydrogen-alpha as blue, since it is a similar wavelength to oxygen-I (which are both red in reality) to create an image reminiscent of the Hubble one, much to my delight.

Whether you are a primarily visual astronomer or a high-tech shutterbug like me, the Crab Nebula is worth spending a little time with this month. Take a moment during your observing to realize how incredible this object is. Rising in the evening hours, it will be up all night for you to enjoy. How much detail can you tease out? Can you spot the pulsar?

Molly Wakeling is an avid astrophotographer active in STEM outreach. She has a Ph.D. in nuclear engineering.

In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear," author and environmental historian Peter S. Alagona looks at the models used to develop the U.S. grizzly bear recovery program, and how California could make an ideal home for a new population.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Computer models are widely used in ecological research and conservation, providing scientists with tools to predict how a given species might respond to a stressor or shift in conditions. These models can then be refined and built upon with real world data to get a better understanding of what's going on within a population and what the biggest risks are.

But models aren't perfect. In this excerpt from "Start With a Bear: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet" (HarperOne, 2026), author Peter S. Alagona highlights how these models are built on the presumptions of their creators. Alagona examines the model of grizzly bear (Ursus arctos horribilis) habitats used by the Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) to inform its recovery plan for the species — and why California, despite its apparent suitability, was left out.

Most of the grizzly habitat models that were introduced in the 1990s and 2000s, and then improved in the 2010s and 2020s, make two key assumptions. They assume that conservation efforts should focus on the best remaining grizzly habitats, and that we can best understand those habitats by studying bears in the places where they still live.

The result has, indeed, been a far better understanding of grizzly habitat use. But this approach has also produced a circular logic with a structural bias toward the status quo. In most grizzly habitat models, past realities and future possibilities fade. With each new study, it seems more and more like the only possible places for grizzlies are the exact kinds of places where they currently live.

The six recovery areas identified in the 1993 Recovery Plan were all places where grizzlies still lived or had recently lived when they were listed as threatened in 1975. The plan argued that these areas "had the potential to provide adequate space and habitat to maintain the grizzly bear as a viable and self-sustaining species." But it also acknowledged the risks and uncertainties facing the bears, and it pledged to assess other areas in their historical range.

This process was expected to take five years. Twenty-eight years later, in 2019, the FWS settled a federal lawsuit in which it agreed to finally conduct this long-delayed analysis. It built a simple model based mainly on secure habitat, and then applied it to both the San Juan Mountains of Colorado and the Sierra Nevada of California. Other potential recovery areas — such as the North Rim of the Grand Canyon in Arizona, the Gila Wilderness in New Mexico, and the Northwest Forest of Northern California — were, for unexplained reasons, not included.

The current grizzly bear recovery zones with the proposed boundaries.

The model did its job. According to the FWS, neither the San Juans nor the Sierra Nevada contained enough secure habitat to support a viable grizzly population. Instead of subjecting the study to peer review, the FWS published it in an appendix on page 286 of a species status report. Having pioneered the idea of secure habitat, David Mattson now set out to explain why the FWS was abusing it. In his view, the service's models focused on artificially small areas, failed to consider several key factors described in the scientific literature, and neglected to conduct essential supporting analyses to explain its conclusions.

The FWS had dragged its heels for almost three decades, and then, after pledging in court to conduct a good-faith analysis, produced a study that seemed designed to reach a predetermined result: The only places capable of supporting grizzlies were the places where the FWS was already trying to recover them. When Mattson and his colleague Troy Merrill ran a more detailed model for the southwestern states, they found that Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah contained seven potential recovery areas with more than 45,000 square kilometers of suitable habitat that could probably support more than 1,000 bears.

For more than a century, the prevailing narrative in California has been that the grizzly's extinction there was inevitable and its recovery is impossible. But Mattson's results for the southwest, combined with California's unique geography, cast doubt on this story.

California is home to nearly 40 million people, and it has more miles of roads than any state except Texas. But its population is extraordinarily concentrated. California is the most urban state, with 95% of its residents packed into cities and 75% living on only around 2% of its land area. Much of California has a human population density lower than that of the Northern Rockies. Unlike in the Northern Rockies, the majority of California's farms are concentrated in broad valleys dozens of miles from core wilderness habitats.

Kings Canyon National Park in California has been identified as one of the locations where grizzlies could thrive.

Outside urban and agricultural areas, California has more protected land than any state except Alaska, including the largest areas of potential grizzly habitat outside the six current recovery zones. Some of these protected areas are in desert ecosystems not suitable for grizzly bears, but others are in mountain ecosystems with potential grizzly habitat.

California's national parks and wilderness areas sometimes strain under heavy visitation, but the numbers paint a complex picture. Consider the southern High Sierra. In 2024, Sequoia Kings Canyon National Park, which is around 865,000 acres and 97% wilderness, topped 2 million visitors for the first time, whereas Yellowstone, which is around 2.2 million acres and 90% wilderness, received almost 5 million visitors, meaning that both parks had about 2.3 visitors per acre. Yellowstone has more than double the total land area in wilderness, but both parks border large U.S. Forest Service wilderness areas and other public lands, and the High Sierra has fewer roads cutting across its protected areas.

In 2024, I coauthored a study, almost eight years in the making, looking at potential grizzly habitat in California. This project, led by Alex McInturff from the University of Washington, ran four computer models, and then compared them to assess the results each produced. One of these models focused on historical sightings of grizzlies in California, two used approaches developed in other regions where brown bears currently live, and one looked at the habitat use preferences of one of California's other large carnivores, the puma.

The Grizzly Bear Recovery Program was created in the 1970s to restore populations to self-sustaining levels.

Each of these approaches has its own strengths and weaknesses. None of them fully account for the distribution or abundance of food on the landscape or for possible conflicts with people. Together, however, they provide a first assessment of the amount, quality, and locations of potential grizzly habitats. Amazingly, about a third of California appeared as suitable habitat in all four models.

The biggest areas of high-quality habitat were in the southern Sierra Nevada, around Sequoia-Kings Canyon National Park, where some of the last California grizzly sightings occurred in the 1920s. The Northwest Forest, along the Pacific Coast near the Oregon border, also scored highly owing to its low human population density and rich forest habitats. The Transverse Ranges, in the state's southwestern corner, scored highly because of their rich chaparral habitats and density of historical sightings, but ranked somewhat lower than the other two because more people live, work, and grow crops, including extensive vineyards and avocado orchards, around its borders.

These results made intuitive sense, given the state's robust historical grizzly population, large areas of protected habitat, and healthy black bear populations. But they represented a departure from the conventional wisdom that dominated the circular logic of most habitat models. For the first time, it was clear how much potential habitat could be available in California for a grizzly recovery. But our approach still clung to the conservative assumption that the grizzly is a wilderness species. We had shown, with some important caveats, that California probably had enough wilderness to support one or more viable grizzly populations.

What we hadn't shown was whether Californians were willing to coexist with grizzlies that might, someday, wander outside the state's wilderness boundaries.

From the book START WITH A BEAR: Humans, Grizzlies, and the Power of Stories on a Crowded Planet, by Peter S. Alagona. Copyright © 2026 by Peter S. Alagona. Published by HarperOne, an imprint of HarperCollins Publishers. Excerpted by permission.

Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.

A century ago, prevailing wisdom cast large carnivores as adversaries—pests and threats to be removed for human safety and prosperity. In North America, among the most targeted of these animals were brown bears, or grizzlies, whose population decimation has made them emblematic of this fear-driven approach to wildlife management.

In California, where they once roamed the land in the tens of thousands, grizzlys have not been seen in more than 100 years. Modern conservation has evolved, yet it often remains rooted in a separation from nature, a systemic opposition that keeps the wild at arm's length.

In Start with a Bear, historian, ecologist, and bear expert Peter Alagona suggests we must reimagine the very heart of conservation, inviting a new framework for sustainable, reciprocal relations with the wild creatures that remain.

Peter S. Alagona is an environmental historian, conservation scientist, and nature-culture geographer. His work explores what happens when people share space and resources (their habitats) with other species: how we interact with non-human creatures, how we make sense of these interactions, why we fight so much about them, what we can learn from them, and how we might use these lessons to foster a more just, peaceful, humane, and sustainable society. He is a professor of environmental studies at the University of California, Santa Barbara. He is the author of "After the Grizzly" and "The Accidental Ecosystem."

#6343. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

#6342. Pakistan’s first astronaut heads for China’s space station

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, Roscosmos is targeting 5:13 a.m. EST to launch the Progress MS-36 cargo ship to the International Space Station (ISS) on a Soyuz-2.1b from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, according to Next Spaceflight. NASA still lists the flight only as no earlier than fall 2026 and has not given a date.

At 5:45 a.m. EST, Arianespace will try again to launch an Ariane 64 from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana with 36 Amazon Leo satellites. A problem with the rocket’s ground support systems halted Monday’s countdown. It is Amazon’s first launch since last week’s Vulcan failure.

Later that morning, at 10:55 a.m. EST, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-266 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force has said what the rocket carries. The booster will land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

That evening, at 7:18 p.m. EST, a Long March 2F is slated to launch Shenzhou-24, carrying three astronauts, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China to the Tiangong space station, per Next Spaceflight.

One seat makes history. A Pakistani astronaut will fly as a payload specialist, becoming the first foreign visitor to Tiangong and Pakistan’s first astronaut. Pakistan’s space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), has shortlisted two pilots, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud. One will fly and the other will serve as backup. The astronaut is expected to spend about a week on Tiangong and return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

On Thursday, Nov. 26, the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) is targeting 4:35 a.m. EST for a Long March 2D launch from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later Thursday, at 7:05 p.m. EST, Rocket Lab will launch Night Owls Never Sleep on an Electron from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula.The payload is a StriX satellite for the Japanese company Synspective. StriX satellites use synthetic aperture radar to image the ground through clouds and darkness.

On Friday, Nov. 27, CASC is targeting 8:00 a.m. EST for a Long March 6A launch from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in Shanxi province, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

On Saturday, Nov. 28, CAS Space, a commercial launch company backed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, plans to launch a Kinetica 1 at 8:00 p.m. EST from a sea platform in the South China Sea, supported by the Haiyang Oriental Spaceport, per Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been announced.

Later Saturday, at 10:50 p.m. EST, a Long March 6C is slated to lift off from Taiyuan, according to Next Spaceflight. Its payload is also undisclosed.

Finally, at 11:39 p.m. EST on Saturday, SpaceX returns to SLC-4E for USSF-380, another classified Space Force mission. The booster is again slated to land on Of Course I Still Love You.

Closing out the week on Sunday, Nov. 29, NASA and Northrop Grumman are targeting 10:47 a.m. EST to launch the NG-25 Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Named the S.S. James A. Lovell after the late Apollo 13 commander, the spacecraft will haul several tons of science and supplies to the ISS.

Last week opened on Wednesday, Nov. 18, at 5:51 p.m. EST, when a Long March 2D lifted off from Taiyuan carrying Shijian-24. China has not said what the satellite does; CGTN reported only that it reached its planned orbit.

On Friday, Nov. 20, at 6:59 a.m. EST, a Long March 8A launched from the commercial launch site at Wenchang with the 30th batch of satellites for Guowang, China’s state-backed broadband megaconstellation.

That night, at 11:20 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-317 mission from Vandenberg, two days later than planned. The booster landed on Of Course I Still Love You.

The week closed on Sunday, Nov. 22, at 7:23 a.m. EST, when a Falcon 9 lifted off from the same pad with the National Reconnaissance Office’s NROL-136, a day later than planned. The launch came 32 hours after USSF-317, SpaceX’s fastest turnaround between launches from the same pad. The booster flew back to Landing Zone 4.

South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development (ADD), the military research arm of its defense ministry, is still preparing the first full demonstration flight of its solid-fueled Mir rocket from an offshore platform near Jeju Island. After canceling a June 30 attempt over safety concerns, the ministry has said only that it aims to launch by the end of the year.

ExPace, a subsidiary of the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation (CASIC), also has a Kuaizhou 11 launch from Jiuquan on the books no earlier than November 2026. Its payload has not been announced.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

Physicists at the Large Hadron Collider have detected a rare, 1-in-10-billion particle interaction that opens a view into the 'zeptoverse,' the smallest distance scale ever measured.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Using the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's largest particle accelerator, scientists have gotten the first glimpse of the "zeptoverse" — the universe as it behaves within less than a hundred-trillionth of a wavelength of visible light, the smallest scale that researchers have explored to date.

The new findings may one day help to answer long-standing cosmic mysteries, such as why there is far more matter than antimatter seen in the universe, and what makes up the dark matter that constitutes about 85% of all matter in the universe, the researchers announced Nov. 3 at a seminar at CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research), the organization that operates the LHC. The study, available as a preprint, has not yet been peer reviewed.

At the LHC, located near Geneva at the border of France and Switzerland, researchers were investigating elusive particles called beauty quarks. These subatomic particles are cousins of the standard "up" and "down" quarks that make up the cores of all atoms in the universe.

When beauty quarks are created — in this case, when the LHC smashes atoms together at incredibly high speeds — they live for just one and a half trillionths of a second before they decay. There are a number of ways beauty quarks can break down; researchers hope that analyzing rare forms of these decays might reveal that they might not unfold as expected.

Such outcomes could then shed light on new kinds of physics found only at very tiny scales of zeptometers, or trillionths of a nanometer. (For comparison, a wavelength of visible light ranges from about 380 to 750 nanometers.)

An artist's visualization of a beauty particle decaying into two muons.

By exploring this zeptoverse, scientists hope to discover new particles that have escaped detection until now.

"We're confident there must be new particles to discover, and these could help explain mysteries like dark matter and the existence of matter in the universe," study co-author Harry Cliff, a particle physicist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Why haven't we seen these particles yet? One answer, and perhaps the most likely answer, is these new particles only become manifest at very, very short-distance scales. So by probing into the zepto scale, we give ourselves the best chance possible of finding these new particles that could explain these mysteries."

We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past.

Now, after hunting for more than four decades, physicists have found the first evidence of the rarest kind of beauty-quark decay seen yet. "Only one in 10 billion beauty particles decay this way," Cliff said.

In this form of decay, technically known as the B0 to mu+ mu− decay, a beauty quark collides with an oppositely charged beauty antiquark. They annihilate each other, generating a pair of smaller particles ‪—‬ a muon and an antimuon. Previous research suggested that this requires a complicated set of interactions, making this kind of decay extraordinarily rare.

An experiment at the LHC called LHCb was specifically designed to study beauty quarks. In 2024, a major upgrade to LHCb made it possible to distinguish different types of particles. Using machine learning techniques, the researchers suppressed huge amounts of background noise, which helped them detect the first evidence of the B0 to mu+ mu− decay.

"We're now recording in a single year what took 10 years to record in the past," Cliff said. "And so we have this massive sample of beauty decays, and that is ultimately what allowed us to see this decay for the first time."

The new results suggest that the way this rare decay happens matches the predictions of the Standard Model of particle physics, the current best description of how the basic building blocks of the universe behave. As such, the researchers have not yet discovered signs of new particles or new physics beyond the Standard Model.

"For me, I think the most exciting thing about this result is the fact that we are probing these unimaginably short distance scales," Cliff said. "Seeing the evidence for this decay begins a new area of research where we can start to make precision measurements that will give us the best chance of finding new physics in the future."

The researchers would now like to upgrade LHCb to fully exploit the improvements to the LHC's luminosity that are currently planned for the 2030s.

"However, there is some doubt over that now because the U.K. recently withdrew funding from the project," Cliff said. "So we are really trying to figure out if we'll be able to continue this type of research."

In an ideal world, "we'll collect many hundreds of these decays in the future, make precise measurements and probe deep into the zeptoverse," Cliff said.
