#6291. Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

It joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft just reached 1 light-day from our planet, but a newfound glitch in the probe's onboard computer is preventing it from sharing science data with Earth.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA has confirmed that its Voyager 1 spacecraft has reached a record-breaking 1 light-day from Earth — but new milestones come with old problems.

On Nov. 14, the Voyager mission team discovered that the nearly 50-year-old space probe had stopped sending science data back to Earth, according to NASA — a problem that the team had to deal with as recently as 2024. As of Thursday (Nov. 19), the team had not resolved the problem.

But they did detect a "carrier" signal that is used to ferry science and engineering information from Voyager 1 to Earth, confirming that the probe is still powered up and pointed in the right direction.

"We have an anomaly that is not unseen before," Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager, said at a NASA news conference Thursday, adding that she is "confident" that the science data will continue flowing again soon.

Using the carrier signal, the team confirmed that the probe had reached its latest distance milestone of 1 light-day from Earth, or roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) away, Wednesday (Nov. 18). At this distance, which no human-made object had ever reached before, it takes a full 24 hours for radio signals traveling at the speed of light to get from Earth to Voyager 1 and vice versa. (The spacecraft's twin probe, Voyager 2, is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035.)

This incredible distance, coupled with the spacecraft's five-decade-old hardware, makes troubleshooting problems on the probe extremely arduous, Dodd explained.

An illustration depicting Voyager 1 at one light-day from Earth.

"It takes two days to diagnose anything with the spacecraft — so we can't do anything fast, and the data rates are very low," she said. "We are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager, just due to the distance and the age."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

According to NASA, the current glitch likely stems from Voyager's onboard computer, which is responsible for collecting data from its science instruments and transmitting it back to Earth in a readable format. The team encountered a similar problem in November 2023 that prevented Voyager 1 from sharing science data until engineers solved the issue in June 2024. The mission team is approaching this new glitch the same way they solved the previous one, NASA wrote in a blog post.

If the fix succeeds, Voyager 1 will continue transmitting data from its two remaining science instruments — a magnetometer, which measures magnetic fields in interstellar space, and a plasma wave detector, which measures charged particles in the interstellar medium. To conserve power on the aging spacecraft, the mission team shut off some of Voyager's instruments earlier this year while powering other, more efficient ones in a "Big Bang" maneuver that should keep the probe alive through at least 2027.

We are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager, just due to the distance and the age

However, it's only a matter of time before Voyager 1 runs out of juice and closes its mechanical eyes to the cosmos. After that, it will continue drifting through interstellar space indefinitely, carrying a Golden Record of images, music and information about life on Earth. In the meantime, Voyager will continue learning everything it can about the strange environment of the interstellar medium — the space between stars, where only Voyagers 1 and 2 have ever been before.

Voyager 1 officially reached interstellar space in 2012, after transforming our views of Jupiter, Saturn and other solar system bodies. For more about the probe's incredible discoveries, check out our collection of Voyager 1's iconic photos.
